delirium.md.tldr: New, fluctuating inattention in a hospitalized patient is delirium until proven otherwise — a medical emergency, not a psychiatric label.
points: Acute onset + fluctuating course + inattention (anchor on arousal and attention).
It almost always has a medical cause — find and fix it.
Reorient and mobilize, restore the sleep-wake cycle, and remove tethers and deliriogenic meds.
delirium.md.cant: Don't sedate your way past it — benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
delirium.md.firstMove: Treat the cause, stop deliriogenic meds, use nonpharmacologic measures; reserve low-dose antipsychotic for dangerous agitation.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old is inattentive and fluctuating two days post-op on oxycodone and diphenhydramine. Best first step?

o.t: Identify and treat the cause; stop deliriogenic meds
Start scheduled lorazepam
Begin donepezil
Reassure the family and observe

quiz.why: This is delirium; the priority is finding the cause and removing contributors (opioids + anticholinergic). Benzodiazepines worsen non-withdrawal delirium.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask baseline cognition, acute onset, fluctuation, sleep-wake reversal, pain, infection, hypoxia, withdrawal, and medication changes.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Prioritize attention and arousal; note fluctuation, disorientation, perceptual disturbance, psychomotor subtype, and cognition.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Treat as medical emergency: remove deliriogenic medications, correct causes, prevent falls, and avoid benzodiazepines except withdrawal.
clinicalWorkflow.say: This looks like a brain-not-working-right-now problem, often from a medical cause, and it usually fluctuates during the day.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family/nursing what is baseline, when it changed, whether it fluctuates, and what helps reorient the patient.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present CAM-style features, likely causes, medication contributors, nonpharmacologic plan, and when medication is needed for dangerous agitation.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Delirium is acute/fluctuating inattention; benzodiazepines usually worsen it unless withdrawal is the cause.

agitation.md.tldr: Treat the driver, not just the behavior — verbal de-escalation before PRN, and PRN before restraint.
points: Secure team and exit safety first.
Check vitals and glucose; rule out a medical cause.
Offer (don't force) oral medication; restraint is the last resort — time-limited and monitored.
agitation.md.cant: Don't reach for an antipsychotic before excluding hypoglycemia, hypoxia, delirium, withdrawal, pain, and akathisia.
agitation.md.firstMove: Lower stimulation, one calm voice, offer oral PRN; IM only if there is imminent danger.

quiz.q: First-line treatment for an agitated patient with normal vitals and no delirium?

o.t: Verbal de-escalation
IM haloperidol + lorazepam
Four-point restraints
Scheduled antipsychotic

quiz.why: Verbal de-escalation is first-line; medication is offered (preferably oral), and restraint is a last resort.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask briefly about pain, fear, intoxication/withdrawal, psychosis, needs, and what would help the patient regain control.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Track arousal, attention, psychosis, intoxication, akathisia, delirium signs, and capacity to engage.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Protect exits, call help early, reduce stimulation, check vitals/glucose, and use restraint only as last resort under policy.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to help, and I also need everyone to stay safe. Let us lower the volume and talk about one next step.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask staff/family what triggered escalation, what has worked before, trauma triggers, and medication reactions.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present driver of agitation, medical rule-out, de-escalation attempts, medication offered, and monitoring/restraint status if used.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Verbal de-escalation is first-line when safe; treat the driver and avoid reflexive sedation.

actions.label: Ask collateral about triggers and what helps

catatonia.md.tldr: Mutism, immobility, posturing, or waxy flexibility — recognize catatonia, do a lorazepam challenge, and hold antipsychotics.
points: Use the Bush-Francis signs; describe motor findings objectively.
The lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
ECT is definitive, especially for malignant catatonia.
catatonia.md.cant: Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia / NMS — exclude those before giving one.
catatonia.md.firstMove: Lorazepam challenge; hold antipsychotics; consider ECT.

quiz.q: A mute, posturing patient with waxy flexibility — best initial step?

o.t: Lorazepam challenge
Start scheduled haloperidol
Physical restraint for safety
Reassure and observe

quiz.why: Catatonia responds to benzodiazepines; antipsychotics risk precipitating malignant catatonia.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask about onset, mood/psychosis, antipsychotic exposure, fever/autonomic signs, seizures, medical illness, and prior catatonia.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Describe motor signs objectively: mutism, stupor, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echophenomena, rigidity, and staring.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Hold antipsychotics until malignant catatonia/NMS is addressed; monitor hydration, nutrition, DVT, autonomic instability, and airway risk.
clinicalWorkflow.say: The stillness and speech change can be part of a treatable motor syndrome, so we are going to assess it carefully.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family/staff what changed, whether the patient eats/drinks, baseline movement/speech, and prior response to lorazepam or ECT.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present BFCRS signs, medical/NMS rule-out, lorazepam challenge plan, supportive care, and ECT escalation threshold.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic; antipsychotics can worsen malignant catatonia/NMS.

t_psychosis.md.tldr: First-episode psychosis is a workup, not a diagnosis — rule out secondary causes before calling it primary.
points: Screen for substances, delirium, autoimmune (anti-NMDA), seizure, and CNS causes.
Characterize positive, negative, and disorganized symptoms.
Choose an antipsychotic by side-effect profile; clozapine for treatment resistance.
t_psychosis.md.cant: Don't anchor on schizophrenia at a first presentation — secondary psychoses are missed when the workup is skipped.
t_psychosis.md.firstMove: Medical workup first; then an antipsychotic chosen by side-effect fit.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old has three weeks of hallucinations, low-grade fever, and orofacial dyskinesias. Most important to exclude?

o.t: Adjustment disorder
Schizophrenia
Malingering
Anti-NMDA receptor (autoimmune) encephalitis

quiz.why: Subacute psychosis with neurologic and autonomic features warrants an autoimmune-encephalitis workup before a primary psychiatric label.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Clarify hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, negative symptoms, mood episodes, trauma, substances, medical/neurologic symptoms, and timeline.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Describe thought process, thought content, response to internal stimuli, affect, behavior, cognition, insight, and judgment without loaded language.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess command hallucinations, paranoia-driven defensive behavior, inability to care for self, access to weapons, and medication adverse effects.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I may not see it the same way, but I can tell this feels frightening, and I want to understand what you are experiencing.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask about first episode vs baseline, substance exposure, medical symptoms, functional decline, family history, and what helps the patient feel safe.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: State primary vs secondary psychosis differential, medical workup, safety drivers, antipsychotic choice, and family engagement plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: First-episode psychosis is a workup; do not anchor on schizophrenia when delirium, substances, seizures, or autoimmune encephalitis fit better.

t_mood.md.tldr: Before treating depression, screen for a past manic or hypomanic episode — antidepressant monotherapy can destabilize unrecognized bipolar illness.
points: Get collateral and ask specifically about prior mania/hypomania (MDQ).
Match severity to setting; consider ECT for severe, psychotic, or catatonic depression.
Lithium carries the strongest maintenance evidence and an anti-suicidal effect.
t_mood.md.cant: Acute mania: stop the antidepressant, start a mood stabilizer or second-generation antipsychotic, and protect sleep.

quiz.q: A patient with prior depressive episodes presents manic while on sertraline. Best next step?

o.t: Add a second antidepressant
Increase the sertraline dose
Stop sertraline; start a mood stabilizer or SGA
Order a brain MRI before any treatment

quiz.why: This is bipolar mania; discontinue the antidepressant and begin an antimanic agent while protecting sleep.

cta.label: Map mania collateral and safety roles

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Anchor depressive, manic, and mixed symptoms to time course; ask about sleep, energy, impulsivity, psychosis, substances, antidepressants, and past episodes.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for psychomotor change, pressured or slowed speech, affect reactivity, thought speed, grandiosity, guilt, psychosis, and cognition.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess suicide, psychosis, inability to sleep, impulsive spending/sex/driving, access to means, and postpartum status when relevant.
clinicalWorkflow.say: It is important that we screen for past mania before choosing a depression medication, because the wrong medication can worsen bipolar illness.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family about decreased need for sleep, episodic behavior change, spending, irritability, psychosis, medication adherence, and baseline functioning.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present unipolar vs bipolar evidence, safety acuity, psychosis/catatonia features, and why today's medication plan fits the risk profile.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Always screen for mania before antidepressants; acute mania means stop antidepressant and start an antimanic agent while protecting sleep.

actions.label: Map mania collateral and safety roles

t_anxiety.md.tldr: SSRIs/SNRIs plus exposure-based therapy are first-line across anxiety, OCD, and PTSD — standing benzodiazepines are a trap on the unit.
points: Rule out medical mimics (hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, substance withdrawal).
OCD: exposure and response prevention plus a higher-dose SSRI.
PTSD: trauma-focused therapy (CPT/PE) is first-line.
t_anxiety.md.cant: Don't start scheduled benzodiazepines for PTSD — they don't treat core symptoms and carry dependence risk.

quiz.q: First-line treatment for OCD?

o.t: Scheduled benzodiazepine
Higher-dose SSRI + exposure and response prevention
Low-dose antipsychotic monotherapy
Supportive therapy alone

quiz.why: OCD responds to ERP and higher-dose SSRIs; antipsychotics are adjuncts, not monotherapy.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Separate panic, generalized worry, obsessions/compulsions, trauma re-experiencing, avoidance, substances, and medical mimics.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for autonomic arousal, avoidance, reassurance seeking, compulsions, dissociation, sleep disruption, and concentration changes.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Ask about suicide, self-harm, substance use, benzodiazepine dependence, domestic violence, and trauma-related vulnerability.
clinicalWorkflow.say: We can ask about trauma at your pace; you do not have to give details for me to understand what feels unsafe now.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask what avoidance or rituals are impairing function and whether symptoms are episodic, trauma-linked, or substance-linked.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present the anxiety/OCD/PTSD syndrome, ruled-out mimics, functional impairment, and why the plan avoids reflexive benzodiazepines.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: OCD is ERP plus higher-dose SSRI; PTSD is trauma-focused therapy; scheduled benzodiazepines are not first-line for PTSD.

t_sud.md.tldr: Time the withdrawal syndrome and treat it proactively — alcohol withdrawal is benzodiazepines (CIWA-guided) plus thiamine before glucose.
points: Use CIWA-Ar (alcohol) and COWS (opioid) to drive symptom-triggered dosing.
Offer medication for addiction: buprenorphine/methadone for opioids; naltrexone/acamprosate for alcohol.
Give thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
t_sud.md.cant: Delirium tremens (48–72h) is a medical emergency with real mortality — escalate early, don't wait.
t_sud.md.firstMove: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine for alcohol; thiamine; begin medication-for-addiction planning early.

quiz.q: On hospital day 2, a heavy drinker is tremulous and tachycardic with visual hallucinations and a clear sensorium. Best management?

o.t: Restraints and observation
Scheduled haloperidol
IV dextrose first
CIWA-guided benzodiazepine + thiamine

quiz.why: Alcohol withdrawal is treated with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines and thiamine before glucose.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask last use, amount, route, withdrawal history, seizures/DTs, overdose, medications for addiction, readiness, and concurrent psychiatric symptoms.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for intoxication, withdrawal, delirium, tremor, diaphoresis, psychosis, mood symptoms, cognition, and pain.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Monitor alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, opioid overdose risk, suicidality, violence risk when intoxicated, and medical instability.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Would it be okay if we talk about what the substance is doing for you and what it is costing you right now?
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Clarify withdrawal timeline, overdose history, access to substances after discharge, family supports, and barriers to medication treatment.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present withdrawal timing, CIWA/COWS trend, thiamine, medication-for-addiction options, and discharge linkage.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Alcohol withdrawal is benzodiazepines plus thiamine; opioid use disorder treatment includes buprenorphine or methadone.

actions.label: Clarify family supports and discharge barriers

t_personality.md.tldr: For borderline personality, the unit's job is a consistent, validating frame — not a medication for the diagnosis itself.
points: DBT-informed stance: validate and hold limits; debrief splitting as a team.
Treat comorbid depression or PTSD; medications target symptoms, not the disorder.
Name and tolerate countertransference rather than acting on it.
t_personality.md.cant: Avoid polypharmacy and reactive medication changes driven by crises — they rarely help and can harm.

quiz.q: Best inpatient response to staff splitting around a patient with borderline personality disorder?

o.t: Discharge for the behavior
Assign one nurse to meet all requests
Start a mood stabilizer for the personality disorder
A unified team plan with consistent, kind limits

quiz.why: Splitting is managed with team consistency and clear limits; medication does not treat the personality disorder itself.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask about enduring patterns, trauma, relationships, self-harm, abandonment fears, affect shifts, and what has helped during past crises.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Track affect intensity, interpersonal stance, impulsivity, dissociation, self-harm cues, and countertransference in the team.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Separate chronic baseline risk from acute change; assess means, intoxication, recent losses, threats, and ability to collaborate on a plan.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to take the distress seriously and also keep our plan consistent, so we do not make reactive changes that later feel unhelpful.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask about baseline risk, effective limits, crisis plans, outpatient supports, and team-splitting patterns without blaming the patient.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present a validating formulation, acute risk change, team consistency plan, and symptom-targeted medication rationale.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Personality disorders are enduring patterns; inpatient care focuses on safety, consistency, comorbidity, and avoiding reactive polypharmacy.

t_neurodev.md.tldr: On the unit, neurodevelopmental disorders (ADHD, autism, intellectual disability) are usually the context a patient arrives with, not the reason for admission — adapt how you communicate and avoid diagnostic overshadowing.
points: Get the developmental and baseline-functioning history from caregivers before interpreting behavior.
Behavior is communication — screen for pain, constipation, infection, and medication effects first.
Treat the comorbidity that actually brought them in (mood, anxiety, OCD, psychosis, catatonia, substance use).
t_neurodev.md.cant: Diagnostic overshadowing — don't write new symptoms off as 'their baseline'; a real change earns a workup. Keep catatonia on the differential in autistic patients.
ruleOut: Undiagnosed mood, anxiety, OCD or psychosis
t_neurodev.md.firstMove: Adapt communication and environment; medical workup for any behavior change; treat the diagnosed comorbidity; psychotropics judiciously (risperidone/aripiprazole for autism-associated irritability).

quiz.q: A nonverbal autistic adult becomes acutely agitated and self-injurious on the unit. Best first step?

o.t: Attribute it to baseline autism and observe
Start a scheduled antipsychotic for the autism
Evaluate for pain and medical causes (constipation, dental, infection) and unmet needs
Place the patient in restraints

quiz.why: Behavior is communication; new agitation or self-injury warrants a medical and functional workup before reflexive sedation — diagnostic overshadowing misses treatable causes.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask baseline communication, sensory needs, routines, developmental history, supports, pain/constipation/infection, and what changed.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Describe communication style, sensory distress, attention, motor findings, affect, behavior, cognition, and possible catatonic signs objectively.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess self-injury, aggression, exploitation, elopement, medical causes, restraint risk, and caregiver capacity.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to understand what usually helps and what may be overwhelming here, not assume this behavior is just baseline.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask caregivers what is new, what communication signals mean, what adaptations work, and what medical issues commonly present as behavior change.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present baseline vs acute change, adaptations needed, medical rule-out, comorbidity target, and restraint-prevention plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Avoid diagnostic overshadowing; new agitation or regression requires medical and psychiatric differential diagnosis.

t_eating.md.tldr: Recognize eating disorders, triage medical instability, and prevent refeeding syndrome — a normal weight never rules out bulimia, and anorexia has among the highest mortality in psychiatry.
points: AN, BN, BED: get weight, orthostatic vitals, temperature, and an ECG; check phosphate/K/Mg.
Decide the level of care by medical instability (bradycardia, orthostasis, electrolytes, QTc), not diagnosis alone.
Refeeding syndrome — start low, go slow, watch phosphate, give thiamine.
t_eating.md.cant: Refeeding hypophosphatemia can be fatal — monitor phosphate/K/Mg daily early and advance calories per protocol; the most malnourished are highest risk.
ruleOut: Comorbid mood, OCD, substance use, suicide risk
t_eating.md.firstMove: Stabilize medically first; multidisciplinary nutritional rehab with supervised meals; FBT (adolescent AN) / CBT-E (BN, BED); fluoxetine 60 mg for BN; no drug is first-line for AN.

quiz.q: A severely malnourished patient with anorexia is admitted and refeeding begins. Which lab change most signals dangerous refeeding syndrome?

o.t: Rising serum sodium
Falling serum phosphate
Falling serum creatinine
Rising hemoglobin

quiz.why: Hypophosphatemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome and can precipitate cardiac and respiratory failure; monitor and replete phosphate (with K, Mg, and thiamine) as calories advance.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask weight trajectory, restriction, bingeing, purging, exercise, laxatives/diuretics, body image, amenorrhea, substances, and medical symptoms.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for anxiety, rigidity, body image distortion, secrecy, cognitive slowing, depression, suicidality, and compulsive exercise urges.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Check vitals, orthostasis, ECG/QTc, electrolytes including phosphate, suicidality, purging complications, and refeeding risk.
clinicalWorkflow.say: A normal weight does not rule out a dangerous eating disorder; the medical risk comes from behaviors and recent change too.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family about meals, exercise, purging, weight change, conflict around food, and ability to support supervised nutrition.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present medical stability, refeeding risk, diagnosis, comorbid mood/OCD risk, nutrition plan, and level-of-care needs.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Refeeding hypophosphatemia is dangerous; anorexia has high mortality and fluoxetine treats bulimia, not weight restoration in anorexia.

t_adjustment.md.tldr: Distress or impairment beginning within 3 months of a stressor and resolving within 6 months of its end — the diagnosis for someone struggling more than expected who doesn't meet criteria for another disorder, and it still carries real suicide risk.
points: If full criteria for MDD, an anxiety disorder, or PTSD are met — it is not adjustment disorder.
PTSD/acute stress disorder require a traumatic event; adjustment disorder follows any stressor.
First-line treatment is time-limited psychotherapy (supportive, problem-solving); medication is adjunctive.
t_adjustment.md.cant: Don't be lulled by the 'subthreshold' label — assess suicide risk directly, as impulsive self-harm can occur.
t_adjustment.md.firstMove: Anchor the timeline to the stressor, confirm criteria for other disorders aren't met, quantify suicide risk, and start brief supportive therapy.

quiz.q: Two months after a divorce, a patient has low mood and impaired work function but does not meet criteria for major depression. Best diagnosis and first-line treatment?

o.t: Adjustment disorder — time-limited psychotherapy
Major depressive disorder — start an SSRI as monotherapy
PTSD — begin trauma-focused therapy
No diagnosis — reassure and discharge without follow-up

quiz.why: Symptoms tied to a stressor, within 3 months, not meeting full criteria for another disorder, indicate an adjustment disorder; supportive/problem-solving psychotherapy is first-line, with suicide-risk assessment.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Anchor symptoms to the stressor, onset within three months, impairment, and whether full criteria for MDD, PTSD, anxiety, or substance-induced disorder are met.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for affect congruence, hopelessness, agitation, sleep change, substance use, and whether symptoms exceed expected coping.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Ask directly about suicide and impulsive self-harm even when symptoms seem subthreshold.
clinicalWorkflow.say: This diagnosis does not mean the distress is minor; it means the symptoms are stress-linked and we still take safety seriously.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask what changed after the stressor, supports, coping, substance use, and whether risk has escalated.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present stressor timeline, excluded full syndromes, functional impairment, safety assessment, and brief therapy/support plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Adjustment disorder requires stressor-linked distress that does not meet criteria for another disorder and resolves after the stressor ends.

t_dissociative.md.tldr: Rule out the medical, seizure, and substance mimics; keep dissociation separate from psychosis and malingering; and stabilize safety before any trauma work.
points: Exclude delirium, seizure, TBI, and substances before diagnosing a dissociative disorder.
Depersonalization/derealization disorder = detachment with intact reality testing.
Suicide/self-harm risk is high — assess it every time.
t_dissociative.md.cant: Don't reflexively start an antipsychotic for dissociative phenomena — no medication treats dissociation itself.
t_dissociative.md.firstMove: Exclude organic causes, ground the patient, assess suicide risk, and treat comorbidities; refer for phase-based trauma therapy.

quiz.q: A trauma survivor reports feeling detached and unreal but knows the feeling isn't real. Best next step?

o.t: Start a scheduled antipsychotic
Grounding and safety, screen risk, treat comorbidities — after excluding organic causes
Begin trauma-processing therapy immediately
Reassure and discharge

quiz.why: Depersonalization/derealization (intact reality testing) is managed with grounding, risk assessment, and comorbidity treatment once organic mimics are excluded; stabilization precedes trauma processing.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask about depersonalization, derealization, amnesia, identity disruption, trauma, substances, seizures, sleep, and neurologic symptoms.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Observe orientation, attention, memory gaps, affective detachment, psychosis markers, and neurologic red flags.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess suicide, self-harm, exploitation, unsafe wandering, intoxication, and trauma-related destabilization.
clinicalWorkflow.say: You do not have to describe trauma details now; I want to understand what happens when you lose time or feel unreal.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask about episodes, triggers, duration, injuries, substance use, seizures, and baseline functioning.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present dissociation vs psychosis vs seizure/substance differential, safety risks, and stabilization plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Rule out seizures, substances, and neurologic causes before diagnosing dissociative disorders.

t_impulse.md.tldr: Look past the behavior for the driver — trace ODD → conduct disorder → antisocial personality disorder, and rule out mania, substances, ADHD, and trauma underneath the aggression.
points: ODD is defiance; conduct disorder violates others' rights; antisocial PD requires conduct disorder onset before age 15.
Episodic aggression with low sleep and grandiosity is mania — not a conduct disorder.
Psychosocial/family interventions are first-line; medication treats the comorbidity, not the 'behavior.'
t_impulse.md.cant: Don't reach for a standing antipsychotic for 'behavior' — screen for and treat mania, substances, ADHD, and trauma first.
t_impulse.md.firstMove: Set a consistent behavioral frame, treat the driving comorbidity, and start parent-management/skills interventions in youth.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old has a lifelong pattern of aggression, theft, and rule violations. Which adult diagnosis requires this history to have begun before age 15?

o.t: Oppositional defiant disorder
Intermittent explosive disorder
Antisocial personality disorder
Bipolar disorder

quiz.why: Antisocial personality disorder (age ≥18) requires evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask what happened before the behavior, developmental history, trauma, ADHD, conduct symptoms, mania, substances, access to weapons, and remorse.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for arousal, irritability, impulsivity, intoxication, grandiosity, paranoia, attention, and capacity for reflection.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess imminent violence, weapon access, target specificity, intoxication, command hallucinations, and environmental triggers.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to understand what set this off so we can reduce risk, not just label the behavior.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family/schools/systems about longstanding patterns, recent escalation, triggers, victims, weapons, and supervision capacity.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present driver of aggression, ruled-out mania/substances/psychosis, violence risk factors, and de-escalation plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Conduct disorder before age 15 is required for antisocial personality disorder; always rule out mania and substances.

t_neurocog.md.tldr: Sort delirium vs dementia vs depression, rule out the reversible causes, and name the subtype — because subtype decides what you prescribe and what you must not.
points: Onset, course, and attention separate delirium (acute, fluctuating, inattentive) from dementia.
Screen every new diagnosis for reversible causes (B12/folate, TSH, CMP, ± RPR/HIV, NPH).
Antipsychotics carry a black-box mortality warning in dementia — and are dangerous in Lewy body disease.
t_neurocog.md.cant: New, fluctuating confusion with inattention is delirium, not 'worse dementia' — work it up before relabeling.
t_neurocog.md.firstMove: Establish trajectory, run the reversible-cause panel, identify the subtype, and treat behavior nonpharmacologically first.

quiz.q: An older adult with dementia has fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. Which is most dangerous to give?

o.t: Melatonin
A cholinesterase inhibitor
A typical antipsychotic (severe neuroleptic sensitivity in Lewy body disease)
Nonpharmacologic reorientation

quiz.why: This is Lewy body dementia; antipsychotics can cause life-threatening neuroleptic sensitivity, so they are avoided or used only with great caution (quetiapine/pimavanserin).

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask onset, course, ADLs/IADLs, medication changes, hallucinations, parkinsonism, vascular history, sleep behaviors, and caregiver burden.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Assess arousal, attention, memory, language, visuospatial function, executive function, psychosis, mood, and gait when possible.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess delirium, driving, cooking, weapons, wandering, exploitation, medication errors, capacity, and caregiver burnout.
clinicalWorkflow.say: The pattern of change helps us separate delirium, dementia subtype, and depression, which lead to different plans.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask caregivers about baseline, functional losses, fluctuations, behavior symptoms, home safety, and realistic supervision.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present syndrome, subtype clues, reversible workup, capacity/safety issues, caregiver plan, and medication cautions.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Lewy body dementia has visual hallucinations/parkinsonism/fluctuations and antipsychotic sensitivity.

t_sexual.md.tldr: Three distinct topics: sexual dysfunctions (check meds first), paraphilic disorders (distress/impairment or non-consent defines the disorder), and gender dysphoria (distress from incongruence — not a disorder of being transgender).
points: SSRIs and antipsychotics are leading causes of sexual dysfunction — review meds before a primary diagnosis.
A paraphilia (interest) becomes a paraphilic disorder only with distress/impairment or harm to non-consenting others.
Gender dysphoria names the distress; use affirming care and screen the elevated suicide risk.
t_sexual.md.cant: Paraphilic disorders involving a child or non-consenting person raise safety and reporting duties.
t_sexual.md.firstMove: For dysfunction, treat the cause (switch to bupropion/mirtazapine, add PDE5i); for gender dysphoria, provide affirming care and continuity; report when a child is at risk.

quiz.q: A patient on an SSRI reports new anorgasmia and distress. Best first step?

o.t: Tell the patient it is unrelated
Diagnose a primary orgasmic disorder immediately
Stop all psychiatric treatment
Address the medication (dose-reduce, switch to bupropion/mirtazapine, or augment)

quiz.why: SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction is common and reversible; manage the medication before diagnosing a primary sexual disorder.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask respectfully about function, distress, medication effects, consent, coercion, trauma, identity, and medical contributors.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Assess shame, anxiety, depression, trauma response, psychosis/mania when relevant, and capacity/consent concerns.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess non-consent, exploitation, violence risk, suicidality in gender dysphoria, and medication/medical contributors.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I ask everyone these questions because medications, mood, trauma, and safety can all affect sexual health.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Collateral is usually limited by confidentiality; involve others only with permission or when safety/legal duties require it.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present the specific domain, medication/medical contributors, consent/safety concerns, and respectful treatment plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Paraphilic disorder requires distress/impairment or harm/risk to others; gender dysphoria is distress from incongruence, not identity itself.

t_sleep.md.tldr: Restoring the sleep-wake cycle is high-leverage — choose CBT-I over hypnotics, screen OSA in treatment-resistant depression, and don't sedate inpatients with benzodiazepines or antihistamines.
points: CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia and beats hypnotics long-term.
Untreated OSA mimics and perpetuates depression — a classic reversible cause of 'treatment resistance.'
Cataplexy = narcolepsy type 1 (low orexin); sleep paralysis/hypnagogic hallucinations are not psychosis.
t_sleep.md.cant: In older inpatients, benzodiazepines and diphenhydramine cause falls and delirium — avoid them.
t_sleep.md.firstMove: Sleep hygiene + CBT-I; treat the specific disorder (CPAP, iron, modafinil, melatonin/clonazepam) and taper offending agents.

quiz.q: A patient with 'treatment-resistant' depression snores, is obese, and is sleepy all day. Best next step?

o.t: Start a long-acting benzodiazepine
Add a third antidepressant
Start nightly diphenhydramine
Evaluate for obstructive sleep apnea (polysomnography) and treat it

quiz.why: Untreated OSA is a common, reversible driver of apparent treatment resistance; diagnose with polysomnography and treat with CPAP before escalating pharmacotherapy.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask sleep schedule, insomnia pattern, decreased need for sleep, nightmares, OSA symptoms, substances, meds, caffeine, and restless legs.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for fatigue vs manic activation, attention impairment, psychomotor changes, irritability, and delirium risk.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess mania, delirium, falls, respiratory risk with sedatives, OSA, substance withdrawal, and suicidality when insomnia is severe.
clinicalWorkflow.say: The goal is to restore the sleep-wake rhythm without using medications that create dependence or worsen confusion.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask nursing/family about actual sleep, nighttime behavior, snoring/apnea, nightmares, and daytime naps.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present sleep syndrome, psychiatric driver, medical contributors, behavioral plan, and medication risk/benefit.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia; decreased need for sleep suggests mania, not simple insomnia.

t_somatic.md.tldr: Treat the suffering without chasing endless workups — the diagnosis rests on the excessive response to symptoms, and the entities separate on two axes: conscious? and external incentive?
points: Somatic symptom disorder is defined by the excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors, not by whether symptoms are 'explained.'
Conversion (functional neurological) is a rule-in diagnosis — Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, non-epileptic seizures.
Factitious = internal (sick role); malingering = external incentive and is not a disorder.
t_somatic.md.cant: Factitious disorder imposed on another is child/vulnerable-adult abuse — a reporting duty; and real disease can coexist, so don't anchor either way.
t_somatic.md.firstMove: Focused workup once, then one consistent clinician with scheduled visits, validation, CBT, and treatment of comorbidities.

quiz.q: A patient has leg weakness that gives way on formal testing but shows a positive Hoover sign. Best framing?

o.t: Tell the patient nothing is wrong
Malingering for disability
Order repeat MRIs until something appears
Functional neurological (conversion) disorder — diagnosed by positive signs

quiz.why: Conversion/functional neurological disorder is a positive, rule-in diagnosis based on internal inconsistency (Hoover sign), not a diagnosis of exclusion.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask symptom timeline, prior workup, illness beliefs, function, reassurance cycles, trauma, mood/anxiety, and substance/medication factors.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for preoccupation, anxiety, functional impairment, affect, insight, and whether symptoms are intentionally produced or not.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess suicide, iatrogenic harm from repeated workups, medication misuse, and missed medical red flags.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I believe the symptoms are real and distressing; our job is to reduce suffering and function loss while avoiding harmful repeat testing.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask outpatient clinicians about completed workups, utilization pattern, functional decline, and helpful communication approaches.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present the medical rule-out, symptom-response pattern, functional impairment, and consistent follow-up plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Somatic symptom disorder is defined by excessive thoughts/behaviors around symptoms, not by symptoms being medically unexplained.

ethics_legal.md.tldr: Confidentiality is the default — know exactly when it yields: a credible threat to an identifiable victim, suspected child/elder abuse, and danger-based commitment — and remember commitment does not equal consent to medicate.
points: Duty to protect (Tarasoff): a serious threat to a reasonably identifiable person overrides confidentiality — warn, notify police, or hospitalize.
Child and elder abuse are mandated reports on reasonable suspicion, not proof; good-faith reporters are protected.
Capacity is clinical and decision-specific; competence is a legal (court) determination.
ethics_legal.md.cant: Involuntary hospitalization does not authorize involuntary medication — refusal stands absent a true emergency or a separate legal process.
ethics_legal.md.firstMove: Default to confidentiality; when risk appears, name which exception applies (identifiable-victim threat, abuse, danger to self) and take the least restrictive protective action — then document your reasoning.

quiz.q: An inpatient tells you he plans to kill his ex-girlfriend when discharged, naming her. What must you do?

o.t: Take protective action — warn the victim and/or notify police, and continue hospitalization
Keep it confidential — HIPAA forbids disclosure
Discharge as planned but document the statement
Ask his family to pass along a warning

quiz.why: A serious threat against a reasonably identifiable victim triggers the duty to protect (Tarasoff): confidentiality yields, and reasonable steps include warning the victim, notifying police, and continued hospitalization.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Clarify the exact ethical or legal question: confidentiality, duty to protect, mandated reporting, capacity, commitment, consent, or refusal.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Document observations relevant to capacity, risk, coercion, intoxication, psychosis, mania, delirium, and ability to communicate a stable choice.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Escalate identifiable threats, abuse concerns, imminent self-harm, grave disability, or urgent refusal of high-stakes medical care to the supervising team immediately.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to protect your privacy, and I also need to explain the few safety situations where clinicians must involve others.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Share the minimum necessary information; ask family or systems partners only what changes risk, capacity, disposition, or mandatory reporting duties.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Name the legal frame, the patient-specific facts, the local-policy dependency, and the supervising/faculty decision still needed.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Capacity is clinical and decision-specific; competence is legal. Involuntary hospitalization does not automatically authorize involuntary medication.

cultural_psychiatry.md.tldr: Elicit the patient's explanatory model, use the DSM-5-TR Cultural Formulation Interview, work through trained interpreters — never family — and guard against documented diagnostic bias.
points: Kleinman's explanatory-model questions surface what the illness means to the patient.
Cultural concepts of distress (e.g., ataque de nervios) can mimic panic or psychosis — ask before you label.
Minority patients are over-diagnosed with schizophrenia and under-diagnosed with mood disorders — a documented bias to guard against.
cultural_psychiatry.md.cant: Never use family members — especially children — as interpreters; book a trained professional and speak directly to the patient.
ruleOut: Misdiagnosis from language or cultural bias
Cultural idiom of distress vs primary disorder
Religious or spiritual experience vs psychosis
cultural_psychiatry.md.firstMove: Ask the explanatory-model questions early, then structure a real cultural formulation with the CFI's four domains.

quiz.q: A Spanish-speaking patient describes sudden trembling, screaming, and a sense of losing control after a family conflict. Her son offers to interpret. Best first step?

o.t: Book a professional interpreter and explore the episode through the patient's explanatory model before assigning a diagnosis
Diagnose panic disorder and start an SSRI
Diagnose brief psychotic disorder and start an antipsychotic
Let her son interpret to save time

quiz.why: This presentation is consistent with ataque de nervios, a cultural concept of distress that can mimic panic or psychosis; a professional interpreter (never family) and the explanatory model prevent mislabeling.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask the patient what they call the problem, what they think caused it, what they fear most, what help they expect, and what would make care feel respectful.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Separate culturally shaped expression from psychopathology; describe affect, beliefs, language, and behavior without assuming your own norm is neutral.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Use trained interpreters for safety questions, assess discrimination/trauma and structural barriers, and avoid family interpreters for confidential or high-risk topics.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I do not want to assume my framework fits yours. Can you tell me how you understand what is happening?
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask about baseline, family meaning, community supports, immigration/language barriers, religious or cultural practices, and what the patient permits sharing.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present the cultural formulation as clinical reasoning: explanatory model, identity/context, supports, barriers, bias risks, and treatment implications.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: DSM-5-TR Cultural Formulation Interview, trained interpreters, and diagnostic bias around psychosis vs mood disorders are high-yield.

ect_neuromodulation.md.tldr: ECT is the most effective treatment for severe, psychotic, or catatonic depression — no absolute contraindications, transient memory effects — and rTMS, ketamine/esketamine, VNS, and bright light therapy each have a distinct niche.
points: Choose ECT when a rapid, definitive response is needed: psychotic or catatonic depression, active suicidality, refusal to eat/drink, pregnancy, or prior ECT response.
Hold benzodiazepines and anticonvulsants pre-ECT (they blunt the seizure), and plan continuation treatment — relapse is the rule without it.
rTMS is outpatient with no anesthesia or memory effects; ketamine/esketamine act within hours and reduce suicidal ideation (esketamine requires REMS monitoring).
ect_neuromodulation.md.cant: There are no absolute contraindications to ECT — raised intracranial pressure and recent MI/unstable cardiac disease are the key relative risks.

quiz.q: A pregnant patient has severe major depression with psychotic features and is refusing food and fluids. Most effective next step?

o.t: Electroconvulsive therapy
Start an SSRI and reassess in 4–6 weeks
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
Bright light therapy

quiz.why: ECT is the most effective treatment for severe/psychotic depression, acts fastest when the patient cannot safely wait, and is safe in pregnancy when indicated.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask about psychotic depression, catatonia, severe suicidality, refusal to eat/drink, pregnancy, prior ECT response, cognitive baseline, and anesthesia/cardiac risk.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for psychomotor retardation, catatonic signs, psychotic guilt, severe mood congruent delusions, cognition, and capacity to consent.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Escalate catatonia, malignant catatonia/NMS concern, inability to eat/drink, or severe suicidal depression where rapid definitive treatment may be needed.
clinicalWorkflow.say: ECT is a medical treatment done under anesthesia; for the right patient it can work faster and more reliably than waiting on medications.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family about prior response, baseline memory, functional decline, fears about ECT, and who can support continuation treatment.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present indication, urgency, capacity/consent status, medical workup needs, medication adjustments, and continuation plan after response.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: ECT is most effective for severe, psychotic, catatonic, or life-threatening depression; there are no absolute contraindications, but relative risks require planning.

t_geri.md.tldr: Separate delirium vs dementia vs depression in every confused elder, treat the reversible, and deprescribe before you prescribe — the drug list is often the diagnosis.
points: Inattention is the fingerprint of delirium — test it at the bedside (digit span, months backward) rather than inferring it.
Effortful 'I don't know' answers with disengagement suggest pseudodementia — treat the depression and cognition improves.
Beers Criteria plus anticholinergic-burden review on every med list; start low, go slow on anything new.
t_geri.md.cant: New psychosis in an older adult is delirium or another medical cause until proven otherwise — work it up before you call it psychiatric.
t_geri.md.firstMove: Test attention formally, get collateral for the true baseline and tempo of change, review every medication against Beers — then treat what's reversible.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old admitted for 'failure to thrive' answers 'I don't know' to most cognitive questions, gives up easily, and stopped cooking after her husband died. A structured cognitive screen is mildly impaired. Most likely explanation?

o.t: Early Alzheimer dementia — start a cholinesterase inhibitor
Depressive pseudodementia — treat the depression and retest cognition
Delirium — search for a UTI
Normal aging — reassure and discharge

quiz.why: Effortful 'I don't know' answers, giving up easily, and a clear mood context are the pseudodementia pattern — cognition improves when the depression is treated. Delirium requires inattention and fluctuation, and dementia patients more often minimize or confabulate than disengage.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Establish baseline cognition, acute change, medications, falls, sleep, pain, infection symptoms, function, and caregiver observations.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Prioritize arousal, attention, orientation, memory, language, executive function, psychosis, affect, and gait/psychomotor change.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess delirium, falls, wandering, medication toxicity, self-neglect, driving/weapons, exploitation, and caregiver capacity.
clinicalWorkflow.say: A sudden change in attention or alertness makes us look for a medical cause before assuming this is dementia or depression.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family what changed from baseline, who manages medications, what home risks exist, and what support is realistic.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present delirium vs dementia vs depression, reversible causes, medication burden, capacity concerns, and discharge supports.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Delirium is acute/fluctuating inattention; dementia is chronic decline; depression can mimic cognitive impairment.

motivational_interviewing.md.tldr: Resist the righting reflex — people talk themselves into change. Use OARS to evoke the patient's own reasons, listen for change talk, and reflect it back instead of arguing.
points: PACE spirit: Partnership, Acceptance, Compassion, Evocation — work with the patient, not on them.
OARS moves: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries — reflecting change talk does the heavy lifting.
Readiness ruler: 'You said 4 — why not a 2?' forces the patient to voice their own reasons for change.
motivational_interviewing.md.cant: Arguing for change (the righting reflex) reliably produces sustain talk — the harder you push, the more the patient defends the status quo.

quiz.q: A patient admitted after his second alcohol-related hospitalization says, 'I'm not an alcoholic.' Which response is most consistent with motivational interviewing?

o.t: 'The labs and your history clearly meet criteria for alcohol use disorder.'
'That label doesn't fit you. And the drinking has landed you here twice this year — what's your read on that?'
'You need to stop drinking or you'll be back a third time.'
'Let's move on to something you're more comfortable discussing.'

quiz.why: A reflection plus a neutral fact and an open question sidesteps the argument and invites change talk. Quoting criteria or issuing warnings is the righting reflex and evokes sustain talk; dropping the subject avoids the conversation the patient actually needs.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask permission before advice: what matters, what worries them, and what would make change feel worth it.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Listen for ambivalence, sustain talk, change talk, affective tone, and whether the patient feels judged or understood.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: If ambivalence involves suicide, violence, withdrawal, intoxication, medication refusal, or discharge risk, escalate the safety question rather than treating it as routine counseling.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Part of you sees a reason to change, and part of you has good reasons to hesitate. What feels most important right now?
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: With permission, ask supports what helps engagement and what conversations predict shutdown, relapse, or nonadherence.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Name the patient's own change language and the next collaborative option; do not present motivation as a fixed trait.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: MI answers reflect, evoke, and ask permission; directive confrontation is usually the trap.

pg_suicide.md.tldr: Ask directly and specifically — thoughts, plan, intent, preparation, means — then separate chronic from acute risk and turn the answers into a formulation, not a checkbox.
points: Ask in plain words: 'Have you had thoughts of killing yourself?' — direct questions do not plant the idea.
Formulate chronic vs acute risk with drivers and modifiable targets — 'denies SI' is not an assessment.
Means safety is specific: firearms, stockpiled medication, who secures them, and how that is confirmed.
pg_suicide.md.cant: Sudden improvement after severe suicidality without a clear explanation is an escalation trigger, not reassurance — as is collateral that contradicts the patient's report.

quiz.q: On hospital day 4, a patient admitted after a serious suicide attempt becomes suddenly bright and calm and asks about discharge. Nothing in the treatment has changed. Best next step?

o.t: Document the improved mood and support same-day discharge
Accept the improvement if the patient completes a safety plan
Treat the unexplained improvement as a possible warning sign — reassess intent, preparation, and collateral before any discharge planning
Avoid re-asking about suicide so the questions don't re-trigger the thoughts

quiz.why: Sudden unexplained improvement after severe suicidality is an explicit escalation trigger — it can reflect relief at a decision to act. A safety plan is one component of the risk plan, not a discharge permission slip, and direct questioning does not implant suicidal thoughts.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask ideation, plan, intent, preparation, past attempts, access to means, protective factors, and what changed today.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Notice hopelessness, agitation, intoxication, psychosis, impulsivity, cognition, and ability to collaborate.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Formulate acute vs chronic risk and escalate disposition decisions to the supervising team and local policy.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I ask directly about suicide because it helps us keep you safe; you will not shock me by answering honestly.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: With permission or safety exception, ask about means, recent behavior, prior attempts, supervision, and discharge environment.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present risk state, risk status, drivers, means access, protective factors, and what supervision or discharge barriers remain.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Do not treat scales as disposition tools; risk assessment is a formulation plus supervised plan.

suicide.md.tldr: Suicide risk assessment is a supervised formulation that turns direct questions, warning signs, means access, and collateral into a safety plan and level-of-care decision.
points: Ask directly about passive death wish, suicidal thoughts, plan, intent, preparation, and access to means.
Separate static risk factors, dynamic treatment targets, and acute warning signs.
Use safety planning and means safety; do not use no-suicide contracts or scale scores as disposition tools.
suicide.md.cant: Do not chart only 'denies SI' or treat a C-SSRS score as a discharge decision; escalate acute risk and disposition questions to supervision and local policy.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask directly about ideation, plan, intent, preparation, past attempts, access to means, protective factors, and what has changed today.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Track hopelessness, agitation, insomnia, intoxication, psychosis, impulsivity, cognition, and ability to collaborate.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Formulate acute vs chronic risk, means access, warning signs, observation needs, discharge barriers, and escalation triggers with the supervising team.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I ask directly about suicide because it helps us keep you safe; you will not shock me by answering honestly.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: With permission or safety exception, ask about means, recent behavior, prior attempts, supervision, and the discharge environment.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present risk state, risk status, drivers, means access, protective factors, collateral, and the supervised plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Direct questions do not implant suicidality; safety plans replace no-suicide contracts, and risk tools do not decide disposition.

violence.md.tldr: Violence risk is a short-term, dynamic, supervised safety formulation: identify static history, current drivers, target specificity, and the least-restrictive plan for the unit right now.
points: Separate static baseline risk from dynamic drivers such as psychosis, intoxication, withdrawal, pain, agitation, or environmental triggers.
Read the escalation curve early: pacing, clenched fists, raised voice, verbal threats, object striking, and blocked exits.
Use room setup, team support, de-escalation, and offered oral medication before restrictive interventions when safely possible.
violence.md.cant: Do not interview alone when concerned, block your own exit, ignore a named target, or treat restraint/involuntary medication as anything other than last-resort, policy-bound safety measures.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask about past violence, current target or victim specificity, weapon access, command hallucinations, intoxication/withdrawal, pain, fear, and environmental triggers.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Track arousal, pacing, voice volume, irritability, paranoia, command hallucinations, intoxication, attention, impulse control, and ability to collaborate.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Interview with team awareness, keep an exit route, reduce stimulation, offer choices and oral medication when safe, and escalate named-target or imminent-risk concerns immediately.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to understand what is making this feel unsafe, and I also need to keep everyone safe while we talk.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask staff, family, and records about prior violence, triggers, weapons, what has helped de-escalate, and any named targets.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present static risk, dynamic drivers, target specificity, unit triggers, de-escalation attempts, and the least-restrictive supervised plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Violence risk is dynamic and contextual; past violence matters, but the immediate driver and target specificity determine today's plan.

t_perinatal.md.tldr: Postpartum psychosis is a bipolar-spectrum emergency requiring urgent admission — a lucid interval does not rule it out; distinguish it from PMADs and baby blues by waxing/waning course, and assess safety for both mother and infant on every encounter.
points: Postpartum psychosis typically appears in the first 1–4 weeks, recurs in 30–50% of subsequent deliveries, and is bipolar-spectrum until proven otherwise — screen for prior mania.
The EPDS screens for depression, not psychosis — ask directly about delusions and perceptual disturbance, and screen for manic symptoms separately.
Stopping maintenance medication in bipolar disorder roughly doubles postpartum relapse risk — 'stop everything' is itself a high-risk clinical decision.
t_perinatal.md.cant: A calm, lucid interval does not rule out postpartum psychosis — the waxing/waning course is the illness, not a sign the crisis has passed.
t_perinatal.md.firstMove: Assess safety explicitly for both mother and infant, screen for manic and psychotic symptoms beyond the EPDS, order TSH and infection workup, and obtain collateral about prior mania or prior postpartum episodes.

quiz.q: A patient 8 days postpartum arrives confused and speaking about her baby being 'replaced.' Her family reports she was completely lucid 3 hours ago. She has a personal history of bipolar disorder. Best next step?

o.t: Reassure the family that the lucid interval confirms the crisis has passed and arrange outpatient follow-up
Admit urgently for evaluation and treatment of postpartum psychosis
Diagnose postpartum depression and start an SSRI
Wait 48 hours to see whether the confusion resolves spontaneously

quiz.why: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency — waxing/waning course with lucid intervals is a feature of the illness, not reassurance. The bipolar history, acute onset, and perceptual disturbance require urgent admission. Starting an SSRI without ruling out bipolar disorder risks destabilization; waiting risks harm to mother and infant.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask pregnancy/postpartum timing, mood, anxiety, sleep, intrusive thoughts, psychosis, bipolar history, supports, feeding, and medication exposure.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Look for waxing/waning psychosis, disorganization, severe insomnia, anxiety, obsessions, guilt, bonding concerns, and cognitive changes.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Assess suicide, infant-harm thoughts, psychosis, inability to sleep, neglect risk, domestic violence, and safe caregiving coverage.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Intrusive unwanted thoughts can be very frightening; I ask directly so we can tell anxiety from psychosis and keep everyone safe.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask partner/family about sleep, behavior change, psychosis, infant safety, medication adherence, and who can provide supervision.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present postpartum timing, PMAD vs bipolar/postpartum psychosis, maternal-infant safety, medication risk/benefit, and support plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency, often bipolar-spectrum, and requires urgent supervised treatment.

nutrition_metabolic.md.tldr: Track metabolic health for every patient on an antipsychotic — weight, glucose, and lipids at baseline, 12 weeks, and annually — and know the dietary safety points for lithium, MAOIs, and grapefruit/CYP3A4.
points: Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden; aripiprazole, lurasidone, ziprasidone, and cariprazine carry the lowest — choose by side-effect profile when efficacy is comparable.
Lithium levels shift with sodium and hydration changes; MAOI patients must avoid tyramine-rich foods (aged cheeses, cured meats, tap beer) to prevent hypertensive crisis.
A Mediterranean dietary pattern is the best-supported food-as-treatment signal for depression (SMILES trial); pair dietary counseling with Motivational Interviewing for sustainable change.
nutrition_metabolic.md.cant: Starting an antipsychotic without documenting baseline weight, glucose, and lipids — and skipping the 12-week recheck — means prescribing metabolic risk without a safety net.
ruleOut: Lithium toxicity from sodium or hydration shift
nutrition_metabolic.md.firstMove: Document baseline weight, fasting glucose, and lipid panel before starting any antipsychotic; counsel MAOI patients on tyramine; check sodium and hydration with lithium; schedule the 12-week recheck at the time of prescribing.

quiz.q: A patient started on olanzapine three months ago had weight, glucose, and lipids checked at baseline. Nothing has been rechecked. What monitoring is now overdue?

o.t: No recheck is needed unless the patient reports symptoms
Weight only — glucose and lipids are checked annually
Weight, fasting glucose, and fasting lipids — the 12-week metabolic recheck is due
A full endocrine panel including cortisol and thyroid — antipsychotics affect multiple hormonal axes

quiz.why: ADA/APA consensus monitoring recommends checking weight, fasting glucose, and fasting lipids at approximately 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic — this is the first scheduled interval recheck, not an annual event. Rechecking weight only is incomplete; a full endocrine panel is not the standard; waiting a full year misses early metabolic drift.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask weight trajectory, appetite, food insecurity, eating patterns, activity, diabetes/lipid history, medication concerns, hydration/salt swings, and access to follow-up labs.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Notice sedation, activation, negative symptoms, binge/purge clues, body image distress, cognition, and motivation or ambivalence around change.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Check antipsychotic metabolic monitoring, lithium hydration/sodium risks, MAOI tyramine counseling, grapefruit/CYP interactions, food insecurity, and eating-disorder red flags.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Metabolic health is part of psychiatric care, especially when the medication that helps symptoms can also change weight, glucose, or lipids.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family or outpatient clinicians about baseline weight, shopping/cooking access, medication adherence, activity, food insecurity, and lab follow-up barriers.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present metabolic baseline, medication risk, labs ordered, nutrition/activity supports, and follow-up responsibility after discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden; antipsychotic monitoring includes weight, glucose/A1c, lipids, and blood pressure.

exp_consult.md.tldr: Frame every consult with the decision that is blocked — then assess capacity (4 Appelbaum abilities), delirium (acute inattention), catatonia (motor signs), and withdrawal (last use plus prior seizure history) before anchoring on any primary psychiatric diagnosis.
points: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific — having a psychiatric diagnosis, disagreeing with the team, or exercising poor judgment in general does not mean lacking capacity for this specific decision.

Delirium is medical until proven otherwise — acute fluctuating inattention demands workup for infection, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, medications, and withdrawal before any psychiatric label is applied.

Catatonia can mimic depression, psychosis, behavior, or refusal — look for mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, and poor oral intake, and escalate rather than assuming oppositional behavior.
exp_consult.md.cant: Accepting 'please evaluate' as the consult question blocks both the consultation and the clinical decision — always name the specific decision at stake and what changed today.
ruleOut: Delirium (rule out reversible medical cause first)
Catatonia (can mimic psychosis, refusal, or depression)
exp_consult.md.firstMove: Name the exact decision at stake, do a brief attention screen and focused MSE, review vitals, labs, and medications for delirium triggers, and escalate immediately for fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, or withdrawal red flags.

quiz.q: The medical team asks psychiatry to 'evaluate' a 68-year-old patient refusing a central line for sepsis. She was lucid yesterday. Today she is intermittently confused, cannot say the months in reverse, and believes her IV is poison. How should the capacity assessment be framed?

o.t: Assess the four Appelbaum abilities for this specific decision — the fluctuating inattention suggests delirium may be impairing capacity reversibly
Diagnose paranoid schizophrenia given the poisoning belief and document permanent lack of capacity
Accept the refusal as a valid patient preference — she has the right to decline
Order a neuropsychological battery before any capacity determination can be made

quiz.why: Capacity is decision-specific: the question is whether she can communicate a stable choice, understand the information, appreciate it applies to her, and reason about options — not whether she has a diagnosis or agrees with the team. The fluctuating inattention suggests delirium as the driver, making the impairment potentially reversible and requiring immediate evaluation.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For consult-style questions, define the question first: capacity, delirium, catatonia, withdrawal, or medication safety.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Match the MSE to the question: attention for delirium, motor signs for catatonia, four abilities for capacity, autonomic signs for withdrawal.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Escalate unstable vitals, delirium, malignant catatonia/NMS concern, severe withdrawal, or refusal with high medical stakes.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to answer the specific consult question and also name what would make this unsafe today.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask team/family for baseline, medical course, treatment refusal context, substance timeline, and prior episodes.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: State the consult question, key data, decision-specific capacity or syndrome assessment, and next supervised step.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Capacity is decision-specific; delirium and withdrawal are medical safety workflows, not purely psychiatric labels.

psychopharm_primer.md.tldr: Choose psychotropics by side-effect profile — metabolic, QTc, movement, prolactin — not recency; monitor proportionally; and recognize the five medication emergencies (serotonin syndrome, NMS, lithium toxicity, QTc/torsades, anticholinergic toxicity) well enough to escalate before decompensation.
points: Antidepressants carry an FDA black-box warning for suicidality through age 24 — not just children; screen for bipolarity before starting any antidepressant, and monitor young adults closely in early weeks.
Lithium has the strongest anti-suicidal evidence in its class and a narrow therapeutic window — levels, renal function, and thyroid monitoring are non-negotiable at every relevant interval.

Clozapine is uniquely effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and requires mandatory ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis; myocarditis, ileus, and lowered seizure threshold are additional red flags requiring immediate escalation.
psychopharm_primer.md.cant: Benzodiazepines left on a scheduled standing basis rather than short-term and targeted create dependence, falls, and delirium — autopilot benzodiazepines are a common and preventable inpatient harm.
ruleOut: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (lead-pipe rigidity + hyperthermia + elevated CK)
psychopharm_primer.md.firstMove: Verify baseline labs are back before a new agent starts, reconcile the medication list for QTc-prolonging and anticholinergic stacking, and escalate any suspected medication emergency immediately — speed matters more than certainty.

quiz.q: A patient on a monoamine oxidase inhibitor and a serotonergic tricyclic develops agitation, tremor, visible clonus, and diaphoresis within 2 hours of a dose increase. The intern considers neuroleptic malignant syndrome. What finding best distinguishes these two emergencies?

o.t: High fever confirms NMS — serotonin syndrome does not cause fever
Diaphoresis alone distinguishes serotonin syndrome from NMS
Rapid onset rules out both — this presentation fits a panic attack
Clonus and hyperreflexia with rapid onset point to serotonin syndrome — NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, and elevated CK over a slower course

quiz.why: The discriminating sign is clonus — rapid-onset clonus with hyperreflexia is the fingerprint of serotonin syndrome. NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, markedly elevated CK, and hyperthermia developing over hours to days on a dopamine-blocking agent. Both can cause fever, so fever alone does not distinguish them. The MAOI-plus-serotonergic-TCA combination is a classic serotonin syndrome setup.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask target symptoms, prior response, adverse effects, medical comorbidities, pregnancy potential, interactions, adherence barriers, and patient goals.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Link medication choice to target findings: psychosis, mania, depression, anxiety, sleep, agitation, cognition, and movement symptoms.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Check metabolic, QTc, EPS/TD, NMS, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, anticholinergic burden, overdose risk, and monitoring needs.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Let us choose based on what we are treating and which side effects matter most to you.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask outpatient clinicians/family about prior trials, adherence, side effects, pharmacy access, and what changed after missed doses.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present target symptom, medication rationale, starting dose, monitoring, side-effect counseling, and backup plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Know signature adverse effects and emergencies: NMS, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, QTc/torsades, and anticholinergic toxicity.

ddx.md.tldr: Run a medical mimic screen before anchoring any psychiatric diagnosis — a new or acutely changed presentation is a medical workup until proven otherwise, especially in elderly, medically ill, and first-episode patients.
points: For new psychosis, delirium is the can't-miss before schizophrenia — confirm attention, get a tox screen and basic labs, and do not assume a primary psychotic disorder on first episode without a workup.
In mania or severe agitation, akathisia — drug-induced restlessness from antipsychotics — is frequently missed because it looks like anxiety or behavioral escalation.
In withdrawal, give thiamine before glucose — a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.
ddx.md.cant: Anchoring on a psychiatric diagnosis before ruling out the medical mimics — especially delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, and thyroid or metabolic causes — is the most common reasoning error on the inpatient unit.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old man with no psychiatric history becomes acutely paranoid, cannot say the months in reverse, and was completely lucid last week. The overnight team labels this 'new onset psychosis' and considers an antipsychotic. What is the most important next step?

o.t: Start a low-dose antipsychotic for the paranoia and request outpatient psychiatric follow-up
Treat as delirium until proven otherwise — check vitals, basic labs, tox screen, medication list, and infection markers before any psychiatric label
Request a psychiatry consult to clarify the diagnosis before doing a medical workup
Schedule formal cognitive testing to differentiate dementia from new-onset psychosis

quiz.why: New confusion with fluctuating attention in an elderly patient is delirium until proven otherwise — the one rule on this page that prevents most errors. Starting an antipsychotic before workup risks masking the medical cause; waiting for psychiatry before doing the evaluation loses critical time; dementia testing is premature when delirium hasn't been excluded.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Start with time course, substances/medications, medical changes, trauma, sleep, and baseline functioning before naming a psychiatric disorder.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Separate observed signs from reported symptoms; note arousal, attention, thought process, perception, affect, insight, and judgment.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Ask the safety trio directly: suicide, violence, and vulnerability/exploitation.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to keep a broad differential at first so we do not miss a medical or substance-related cause.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family or outpatient clinicians what is new, what is baseline, and what changed right before admission.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present symptoms, syndrome, leading diagnosis, dangerous alternatives, and what data would change your mind.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Shelf questions often hide medical mimics, substance causes, and medication adverse effects inside psychiatric vignettes.

pg_interview.md.tldr: Use the interview as a circle with the patient's story at the center — covering all 11 domains in whatever order the conversation allows — and always gather the safety trio (suicide, violence, vulnerability) before closing.
points: Ask suicide questions directly: 'Have you had thoughts of killing yourself?' — direct questions do not implant suicidal thoughts, and indirect approaches miss real risk.

MSE language should be behavioral and observable: write 'affect constricted, minimally reactive, mood-congruent' rather than 'patient appeared depressed' — describe what you saw, not your interpretation.
Close every interview with a summary in the patient's language, one correction invitation, and one named next step — this closes the loop and builds trust.
pg_interview.md.cant: 'Denies SI/HI — no risk' is not a risk assessment; document what you asked, what the patient reported, and the reasoning that led to your risk level.

quiz.q: During a rounds presentation, a student reports: 'On MSE, mood was depressed and the patient was anxious.' The attending asks for more precise language. Which revision is best?

o.t: The patient appeared to have a depressed mood and showed signs of anxiety
Patient denied euphoria and grandiosity; affect within normal limits
Mood: 'really low, like a 2 out of 10' (patient quote); affect constricted, minimally reactive, mood-congruent; no psychomotor agitation
Patient reported moderate depression and anxiety consistent with major depressive disorder

quiz.why: The MSE separates mood (the patient's subjective report, always quoted in the patient's words) from affect (the clinician's behavioral observation: range, reactivity, congruence). Option 3 shows both correctly. The other options either interpret rather than observe, skip the patient quote, or make a diagnostic statement where a description belongs.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Open with the patient story, then loop through mood, psychosis, anxiety/trauma, substance use, cognition, medical causes, and safety.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Observe from the first moment: engagement, psychomotor activity, speech, affect range, thought form, perception, cognition, insight, and judgment.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Before closing, ask directly about suicide, violence, grave disability, abuse, and access to means.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I will ask some direct safety questions because they help us take good care of you here.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask permission when possible; explain confidentiality limits and why collateral helps establish baseline and safety.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Report what the patient said, what you observed, what you still need, and what safety questions were answered.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Interview questions test next best question, safety closure, and whether you can distinguish patient report from MSE observation.

pg_formulation.md.tldr: Answer why-this-person, why-this-syndrome, and why-now using the four-layer framework (body/brain, psychiatric syndrome, relationships/environment, recovery/role) — a diagnosis without a formulation is just a label.
points: The five-part differential always includes substance/medication-induced and medical contributors — stopping at the primary psychiatric diagnosis skips the most reversible causes.
The formulation template: name the leading syndrome, the contributors from each layer, the immediate risk, and what must change before discharge — then explain how the treatment follows from that.
Faculty questions that sharpen formulation: 'What would make this diagnosis wrong?' and 'What collateral would change the plan?' — bring answers to these before presenting.
pg_formulation.md.cant: Listing a diagnosis without a formulation leaves the team without the why-now — and without the why-now, the treatment plan has no clinical logic.

quiz.q: A student presents a patient with severe depression and recommends starting an SSRI. The attending asks for the formulation before any treatment decision. What must the student add?

o.t: A summary of the body/brain contributors, the psychiatric syndrome, the family/social context, what must change before discharge, and how the SSRI fits that picture
The specific DSM criteria met by the patient
A list of prior antidepressants the patient has tried and why they failed
The patient's GAF score and number of prior hospitalizations

quiz.why: A formulation answers why-this-person, why-this-syndrome, and why-now — linking those answers to the treatment choice. The four-layer framework (body/brain, syndrome, relationships/environment, recovery/role) is the structure. The SSRI is only clinically reasoned after the formulation confirms the target is a primary depressive episode, not bipolar depression, a substance-induced condition, or a medically driven one.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask what made this person vulnerable, what precipitated this admission, what perpetuates symptoms, and what protects recovery.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use the MSE to support or challenge your formulation, not just to fill a template.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Formulate risk dynamically: baseline risk, acute change, protective factors, access to means, and supervision needs.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Here is how I am understanding why this is happening now, and I want to check that with you.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Look for relational patterns, housing/financial stressors, medication access, and family capacity.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Give a one-sentence formulation before your plan: syndrome plus context plus immediate treatment target.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Distinguish symptoms, syndromes, diagnoses, formulation, and treatment targets.

doc_oral.md.tldr: Write notes and give presentations that reveal reasoning — every note should let the next clinician know what you are treating, what else it could be, what the risk is today, what changed, and what has to happen before discharge.
points: Daily rounds presentations run 60–90 seconds: hospital day, overnight events, one subjective point and one MSE change, a risk update, and a plan question — lead with what changed, not the full history.
Organize the note plan by problem: safety → medications/medical/substance/sleep → psychotherapy/milieu → family/collateral → disposition — so the structure mirrors the clinical priorities.
