The handoff template names the main overnight risks, a trigger-plan pair (if X happens, do Y), and what escalates and what helps with this patient — generic handoffs create coverage gaps.
Practice two micro-updates out loud: a 30-second collateral update and a 60-second rounds update.
doc_oral.md.cant: Copying forward yesterday's risk language without updating the reasoning — 'denies SI/HI, low acute risk' on hospital day 7 without noting today's context — erases the clinical event and creates a documentation gap.

quiz.q: During a 90-second rounds update, a student presents 5 minutes of history and ends with 'so the plan is to continue current medications.' The attending asks what the student should have led with instead. What is correct?

o.t: A full review of the patient's psychiatric history to give the team context
The complete medication list with doses and adherence
A review of the patient's insurance and discharge plan
Hospital day, what changed overnight, one MSE point, a risk update, and the clinical question for the team

quiz.why: A daily rounds presentation is a structured 60–90 second clinical update — it begins with the hospital day and what changed overnight, not a retelling of the history. The attending already knows the background; they need to know what shifted and what decision is needed today. A plan question names the uncertainty and invites attending input.

cta.label: Open the Formulation & DDx Pocket Guide

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Before rounds, ask what changed overnight, what data are missing, what risk changed, and what decision the team needs today.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Report MSE findings that support the assessment, especially changes from yesterday and safety-relevant observations.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Always include current suicide/violence/vulnerability risk, observation level, restrictions, and discharge barriers when relevant.
clinicalWorkflow.say: My assessment is... because... and the next decision is...
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Include collateral only when it changes diagnosis, risk, treatment, or discharge planning.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Use problem representation, focused interval events, MSE delta, assessment, and prioritized plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Oral presentations reveal clinical reasoning: what changed, why it matters, and what you will do next.

exp_tx.md.tldr: Every treatment decision starts with a target symptom linked to the formulation — name what the intervention is treating and why it fits, monitor for adverse effects, and remember that inpatient treatment is medication plus supportive therapy plus milieu plus family.
points: Treatment rationale template: 'The main target is [symptom/risk]; I think [intervention] fits because [formulation reason]; the main monitoring need is [X]; the discharge implication is [Y].'
Inpatient treatment is not just medication — monitor sleep schedule, group attendance, PRN use, and family calls that worsen or improve regulation as clinical data equal in weight to the medication.
Ask what the patient has tried before, what helped, what caused adverse effects, and what medication belief or fear needs to be addressed — prior history changes the choice.
exp_tx.md.cant: Recommending a medication without naming the target symptom or the formulation reason — 'continue olanzapine' without linking it to a specific symptom target — is not a treatment plan.

quiz.q: A student recommends olanzapine for a patient admitted with acute psychosis. The attending asks for the treatment rationale. Which response demonstrates the required reasoning?

o.t: Olanzapine is an atypical antipsychotic with established efficacy for schizophrenia
The main targets are persecutory delusions and sleep disruption driving acute risk; olanzapine addresses both; monitor baseline weight, glucose, and lipids given metabolic burden
The patient has failed two other antipsychotics, so olanzapine is the next logical step
The family requested this medication and the patient tolerated it well in the past

quiz.why: A treatment rationale links a specific target symptom to the formulation, names why the intervention fits, identifies the monitoring need, and implies the discharge plan. Naming the drug class without the target is not a rationale; prior failures change choice but are not the rationale; family request and past tolerance are clinical data, not sufficient justification on their own.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For every intervention, ask the target symptom, target risk, prior response, adverse-effect risk, patient preference, family/system barrier, and discharge implication.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Link the plan to observed targets: sleep, psychosis, mania, depression, anxiety, cognition, behavior, alliance, and functional participation.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Check monitoring, toxicity, withdrawal, overdose risk, falls, QTc/metabolic/EPS risks, and whether the plan depends on local order sets.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Let us name what this treatment is meant to help, what could go wrong, and what would tell us it is working.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family or outpatient clinicians about previous trials, adherence barriers, side effects, practical supports, and what made past plans fail.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present treatment as target plus rationale plus monitoring plus discharge consequence.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Treatment questions reward matching diagnosis, acuity, contraindications, side effects, and patient-specific barriers rather than choosing the newest medication.

exp_family.md.tldr: Discharge risk peaks in the first week post-discharge — map every barrier (housing, medications, follow-up, family capacity, means safety) before any note says 'plan for discharge,' and always leave with a scheduled 7-day appointment, not a phone number.
points: Suicide risk in the first week post-discharge is roughly 100× the population rate — a pre-scheduled 7-day follow-up appointment (not 'they will call to arrange one') is itself an evidence-based intervention.
Structured lethal-means counseling cut attempts and deaths from 3.3% to 0.83% at 180 days — 'who can confirm items are secured before discharge?' is a clinical act, not a formality.
Family involvement during admission nearly triples the odds of 7-day follow-up, and family psychoeducation lowers 12-month relapse from ~37% to ~10% — bringing family in is treatment, not logistics.
exp_family.md.cant: 'The family is supportive' is an observation, not a discharge plan — verify concretely who can do what (medications, transportation, means safety, appointments) before any note says 'safe for discharge.'

quiz.q: A patient with a recent serious suicide attempt is being discussed for discharge. The team notes 'family is supportive and patient has a safety plan.' What is the most important missing element before discharge planning proceeds?

o.t: A PHQ-9 score below 10 to confirm symptom resolution
Written confirmation that the patient has memorized the safety plan steps
A discharge barrier map confirming housing, medication access, a scheduled 7-day follow-up appointment, and confirmed means restriction
An attestation from family that they have read the diagnosis handout

quiz.why: 'Family is supportive' is a conclusion, not a plan. The discharge barrier map must verify specific domains: where the patient will sleep, who will be there, whether medications are obtainable, whether a 7-day appointment is actually scheduled, and who has confirmed lethal means are secured. Each unconfirmed assumption is a gap in the safety net.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask who is involved, what support is realistic, what barriers exist, what worries family most, and what safety role they can actually play.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use patient interaction with family to observe affect regulation, psychosis, insight, conflict patterns, and alliance ruptures.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Clarify means safety, medication access, supervision, housing, transportation, follow-up, and what would trigger urgent return.
clinicalWorkflow.say: We can plan better if we name what the family can do, what they cannot do, and what the treatment team remains responsible for.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask better collateral questions: baseline, recent change, risk behaviors, adherence, strengths, barriers, and family limits.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present discharge barriers, family capacity, safety plan, follow-up, and what still must be solved before discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Discharge safety is a systems task; a phone number is not the same as a scheduled follow-up plan.

family_modalities.md.tldr: Match the family intervention to the family in front of you — family psychoeducation is the default highest-evidence approach (OR 0.18, NNT 7 for relapse prevention), but dose matters: ≤2 sessions is ineffective, and the main barrier to delivery is clinician avoidance, not patient refusal.
points: Family psychoeducation (OR 0.18 vs. treatment as usual) is the single strongest psychosocial intervention for schizophrenia relapse prevention, supported by 90 RCTs across more than 10,000 patients.

CRAFT is the go-to modality when a family member is struggling with a patient's substance use — it changes the family's own behavior to reduce blame and invite treatment engagement, without confrontation.
Expressed emotion (high criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement) roughly quintuples relapse odds; family warmth is protective — lowering expressed emotion is a modifiable clinical target.
family_modalities.md.cant: ≤2 family sessions is ineffective for relapse prevention — NICE recommends ≥10 sessions over ≥3 months; a single discharge meeting starts the work but is not a course of care.

quiz.q: A patient with schizophrenia is preparing for discharge. Family members are willing to participate in family work. Which intervention has the strongest evidence for preventing 12-month relapse?

o.t: Family psychoeducation — OR 0.18 for 12-month relapse across 90 RCTs, with ≥10 sessions over ≥3 months required for the effect to hold
Emotionally Focused Therapy — attachment-based approach targeting the pursue-withdraw cycle in couples
A single family meeting covering diagnosis and the safety plan before discharge
Solution-focused brief therapy — one high-yield session amplifying existing family strengths

quiz.why: Family psychoeducation has the strongest evidence for schizophrenia relapse prevention (OR 0.18 vs. treatment as usual; 90 RCTs, >10,000 patients). EFT is evidence-based for couples but is not the default for schizophrenia; a single meeting is below the therapeutic dose (≤2 sessions is ineffective); solution-focused therapy is useful when only one meeting is possible but does not have the relapse-prevention evidence base.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Before inviting family work, ask what the patient wants help explaining, what the family is worried about, and whether family involvement is safe and welcome.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Notice interactional data: criticism, warmth, emotional over-involvement, guardedness, shame, and the patient's response to family presence.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Family involvement must respect consent, confidentiality, violence risk, coercion, and local policy; do not use relatives as substitutes for clinical supervision or crisis response.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Name the family intervention in ordinary language: 'This is a structured meeting to lower stress, agree on warning signs, and make the discharge plan realistic.'
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Gather timeline, baseline functioning, relapse signatures, adherence barriers, access to lethal means, caregiver capacity, and what has made conflict better or worse.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Report one family-system finding that changes the plan: expressed emotion, discharge feasibility, safety environment, or who needs the next call.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Know that family psychoeducation has the strongest relapse-prevention evidence in schizophrenia and requires more than one brief meeting.

family_playbook.md.tldr: Structure the 90-minute meeting across five phases — open/join, share the picture, hear the family and read expressed emotion, problem-solve and plan, then summarize — convene early to plant a seed, not at discharge to harvest one.
points: Convene the family meeting early in the admission — the relapse-prevention benefit of family work accrues over the following 12 months, not on the unit; saving it for the day before discharge squanders the inpatient window.

Phase 3 (0:35–0:55) — hearing the family's perspective and reading expressed emotion — is the phase that most changes outcomes; protect the time, listen without correcting in the moment, and de-shame by framing behavior as regulation, not character.

Set the meeting goal in one sentence before you begin: 'Align on the diagnosis and discharge plan' or 'Lower the temperature and agree on warning signs' — a meeting with a single clear goal beats one that tries to cover everything.
family_playbook.md.cant: Letting information-sharing (Phase 2) expand to fill the entire meeting is the most common failure — the clinical work that changes outcomes is in Phase 3 (family perspective) and Phase 4 (shared planning), not the didactic.

quiz.q: A family meeting has run to 85 minutes. The team shared the diagnosis and treatment plan thoroughly but skipped Phase 4 (problem-solving) and Phase 5 (close). With 5 minutes remaining, what should the facilitator prioritize?

o.t: Re-review the diagnosis and medication rationale so the family leaves with complete information
Schedule a separate follow-up meeting to complete the missed agenda items
Open the floor for family questions about long-term prognosis
Summarize one concrete shared agreement, name the next contact, and close — even an incomplete meeting with a shared next step is more durable than leaving without one

quiz.why: Phase 5 (close, last 10 min) anchors the meeting: recap the plan in the family's own words, name the follow-up, and hand over a written version. A meeting that ends without a shared next step loses its durability. Over-investing in information delivery at the expense of Phases 3 and 5 is the classic pitfall the page names.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Before the meeting, ask the patient what they want shared, what they fear, and what the family most needs to understand.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: During the meeting, observe alliance, expressed emotion, blame, fear, grief, and the patient's ability to participate.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Clarify confidentiality, means safety, crisis steps, supervision limits, and whether family involvement is helpful or harmful.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to start by making sure we share the same goal: understanding what happened and what needs to be safer after discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Invite family observations without turning the meeting into cross-examination; ask for examples and changes from baseline.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Report meeting goals, what family can support, unresolved conflict, safety commitments, and next system tasks.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: High expressed emotion worsens relapse risk; psychoeducation and structured family work can reduce relapse in psychosis.

brief_psychotherapy.md.tldr: Match the technique to the mechanism — behavioral activation for shutdown/anhedonia, safety planning for suicidal states, psychoeducation for illness confusion — rather than choosing a school; the modality matters less than the fit.
points: Behavioral activation is the highest-yield, lowest cognitive-demand inpatient move for the withdrawn anhedonic patient — it works by scheduling one small valued activity, not by asking a depressed person to think their way out.
Psychoeducation has the strongest inpatient numbers: readmission NNT 5, relapse NNT 9 — give it as a conversation with family looped in, not a packet dump.
Safety planning with follow-up reduces suicidal behaviors by approximately 50%; no-suicide contracts have no evidence and create false reassurance — abandon them.
brief_psychotherapy.md.cant: No-suicide contracts have no evidence and can create false reassurance — replace every contract with a collaborative safety plan in the patient's own words, with a scheduled follow-up contact.

quiz.q: A patient admitted after a suicide attempt is now medically stable but withdrawn, has stopped attending groups, and says 'nothing matters.' The student wants to do a brief bedside intervention. What is the best match for the mechanism driving the crisis?

o.t: Cognitive restructuring — identify and challenge the automatic thoughts driving hopelessness
Behavioral activation — schedule one small, concrete, valued activity; behavioral shutdown responds better to action than to thought-change in the acute setting
Chain analysis — walk the sequence leading to the suicidal crisis to understand its function
Motivational interviewing — roll with ambivalence about treatment and evoke change talk

quiz.why: The mechanism is behavioral shutdown — withdrawn, anhedonic, inactive. Behavioral activation is the match: it targets this mechanism directly by scheduling activity and requires the lowest cognitive demand, which is why the page flags it as the best inpatient fit. Cognitive restructuring requires cognitive engagement a deeply depressed patient may not have; chain analysis is for a self-harm incident; MI is for motivational ambivalence.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask what feels most urgent today, what they have tried, what helps even a little, and what would make the next hour safer or more tolerable.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use affect, thought process, defenses, alliance, and readiness to choose supportive, CBT, DBT-informed, or MI micro-skills.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Keep bedside therapy within scope: stabilize, validate, problem-solve, and escalate risk or trauma flooding to supervision.
clinicalWorkflow.say: We may not solve everything today, but we can make the next step clearer and less lonely.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask the team what pattern they are seeing and align the intervention with the shared treatment frame.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present the skill used, patient response, risk change, and what the team should reinforce consistently.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Supportive therapy strengthens coping and alliance; DBT-informed inpatient work emphasizes validation plus limits.

evidence_inpatient.md.tldr: The strongest inpatient evidence: environmental safety checklists cut inpatient suicide 82%; brief CBT (up to 4 sessions) reduces post-discharge attempts 60% (NNT 7); family psychoeducation cuts 12-month relapse (OR 0.18); antipsychotics do not improve delirium outcomes.
points: MIND-USA (n=566) and AID-ICU (n=1,000) both found no benefit for antipsychotics vs. placebo on delirium outcomes — the PADIS guidelines recommend against routine antipsychotic use for delirium.

The VHA MHEOCC environmental safety checklist produced an 82% reduction in the inpatient suicide rate — ligature point removal is the single strongest structural inpatient suicide prevention intervention.

Pre-discharge 7-day follow-up (actually scheduled, not 'patient will call') is associated with substantially lower suicide risk, and family involvement during admission nearly triples the odds of achieving it.
evidence_inpatient.md.cant: Antipsychotics for non-withdrawal delirium — the MIND-USA and AID-ICU trials showed no benefit; reserve them for severe hyperactive delirium refractory to non-pharmacological bundles.

quiz.q: A 72-year-old develops hyperactive delirium 2 days after hip surgery. The surgical team asks whether starting haloperidol is appropriate. What does the strongest evidence support?

o.t: Haloperidol is first-line for hyperactive delirium and should be started promptly
A low-dose atypical antipsychotic is preferred over haloperidol for delirium because it is better tolerated
Non-pharmacological multicomponent bundles are first-line; antipsychotics showed no benefit in MIND-USA and AID-ICU and should be reserved for severe refractory hyperactive symptoms
Benzodiazepines are the evidence-based first choice for non-withdrawal delirium

quiz.why: MIND-USA and AID-ICU both showed no benefit for antipsychotics vs. placebo on days alive without delirium or coma; the PADIS guidelines recommend against routine use. Multicomponent non-pharmacological bundles (HELP-based) reduced incident delirium by 53%. Benzodiazepines are reserved for alcohol/benzo withdrawal delirium — they worsen non-withdrawal delirium.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Use one evidence question from today's patient: What changes safety, disposition, medication choice, or family counseling?
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Separate observable inpatient outcomes (agitation, sleep, participation, delirium signs) from symptom labels and trial endpoints.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Treat guideline and trial summaries as teaching support only; confirm orders, observation level, legal steps, and discharge requirements with the attending and local policy.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Translate the evidence into one plain-language sentence a patient or family could understand, without overstating certainty.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask collateral questions that affect the evidence-based plan: prior response, adherence barriers, safety environment, firearms/ligatures, family capacity, and follow-up realism.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Bring one trial, guideline, or source-backed number only if it changes the plan; otherwise keep the presentation clinically focused.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Link each landmark finding to a shelf-style distinction: delirium treatment, suicide prevention, capacity, family psychoeducation, or risk prediction limits.

protocol_library.md.tldr: A teaching index of the unit's order sets — always pull exact medications, doses, and monitoring from the live EHR order set; this page tells you which protocol applies and why, not what to prescribe.
points: Withdrawal protocols use symptom-triggered scoring (CIWA-Ar for alcohol/benzo, COWS for opioids); always give thiamine before glucose in any withdrawal or nutritional risk.
Clozapine initiation requires mandatory ANC monitoring per the hematologic schedule — know the workflow before the patient starts, not after the first dose.
Delirium prevention bundles non-pharmacologic measures first; the restraint and agitation pathway is least-restrictive, time-limited, and always followed by a debrief.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Identify which protocol applies, what clinical threshold activates it, and what patient factor makes the standard pathway unsafe or insufficient.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use MSE and bedside findings to support the protocol question: attention for delirium, motor signs for catatonia, arousal for withdrawal, and risk state for safety protocols.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Do not use this page as an order set; exact medications, doses, monitoring, and escalation steps must come from the live EHR/local policy and supervising clinician.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I am going to check the current order set and the team plan rather than relying on memory for protocol details.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask nursing, pharmacy, social work, and outpatient clinicians for protocol-relevant history: prior withdrawal severity, clozapine monitoring, safety planning, and discharge barriers.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: State the protocol, why it applies, the live order set or policy source, and what exception or monitoring issue needs senior review.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Know the conceptual indications and safety logic; local protocol details are not shelf facts and should not be guessed.

welcome.md.tldr: Start with orientation, then use Today / Progress for repeat visits — the hub is meant to answer what to do before rounds, after rounds, before leaving, and before exam study.
points: First visit: open the orientation packet and learn the safety/supervision boundaries before using bedside tools.
Repeat visits: use Today / Progress to choose one ward task, one practice drill, and one review item.
Nothing here replaces supervision; the hub should help you ask better questions and escalate earlier.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Before you open a patient page, ask what you need right now: orientation, bedside action, communication rehearsal, rounds prep, or shelf review.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use the MSE tool when you need language for what you actually observed rather than a generic descriptor.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: If the question is immediate suicide, violence, withdrawal, delirium, catatonia, or capacity, escalate to supervision before studying around it.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I am using the hub to prepare my questions and presentation, but I will bring safety or treatment decisions to the supervising team.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Keep patient identifiers out of notes, tools, search, AI, or exports; use fictional or fully de-identified practice only.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Pick one page, one tool, and one question to bring to the team rather than trying to read the whole library.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Use shelf mode and daily review for retrieval practice; use patient pages to organize the facts.

orientation.md.tldr: One safety rule above all: if you are worried about immediate safety, tell the resident or attending now — do not wait, do not carry it alone; the four daily questions, PHI discipline, and student boundary rules structure everything else.
points: Escalate immediately for: current suicidal intent or new plan, threats or escalating agitation, confusion/fever/rigidity suggesting delirium or catatonia, or any withdrawal concern — these cannot wait for rounds and belong in Week 1 safety recognition.

Use four questions for every patient: what is the syndrome? What medical/substance/sleep/medication factor is driving it? What family/social/discharge context changes the plan? What must be safer before discharge?

Students may interview patients, draft notes, suggest differentials, and observe family meetings with a defined role — but may not make independent safety or discharge decisions, promise anything, or provide unsupervised therapy.
orientation.md.cant: PHI leaves the clinical system in any form — not into AI tools, personal notes, cloud docs, texts, or email; the PHI firewall is absolute and applies to every device and platform.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For every patient, ask what syndrome is present, what is driving it, what family/discharge context matters, and what must be safer before discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Start with observable behavior, speech, mood/affect, thought process/content, perception, cognition, insight, and judgment.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Tell the resident or attending immediately for current suicidal intent, threats/escalating agitation, delirium/catatonia signs, or withdrawal concern.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I am a medical student on the team. I will share safety concerns with my supervising clinicians, and I want to understand what would help you feel safer here.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask permission for collateral when possible; if safety requires it, use the minimum necessary information and involve supervision.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present one patient with syndrome, driver, risk, family/discharge context, and the one question you need help answering.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Orientation facts become exam reasoning when you connect safety, capacity, confidentiality, and supervision boundaries.

core_readings.md.tldr: Fourteen hub pages form the spine of the rotation — read these and you will have covered the core diagnostic classes, the acute can't-miss calls, one medication primer, one family/therapy module, and one differential reasoning scaffold.
points: Start with the acute and safety pages before the diagnostic classes — suicide risk, agitation, and consult essentials are the can't-miss calls you will face from Week 1.
Two pocket cards belong on your person every day: the Interview & MSE guide and the Formulation & DDx guide — they replace the improvised checklist on rounds.
The differential-diagnosis scaffolds and rounds questions pair with the landmark trials audio set for the deepest shelf and COMAT preparation in the hub.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Pick the next core reading by the patient problem in front of you: safety, diagnosis, medication, family/system, or formulation.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Pair each diagnosis reading with one observed MSE feature you can describe on rounds.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Read the acute/safety spine first when the ward problem involves suicide, agitation, delirium, withdrawal, catatonia, capacity, or violence.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I am going to read the page that matches this patient's immediate clinical question, then bring one uncertainty back to rounds.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use readings to sharpen collateral questions: baseline, timeline, adherence, family role, and discharge feasibility.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Turn each reading into one sentence you can use in a patient presentation or plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: After reading, test the same topic with active recall or practice questions within 24 hours.

week1.md.tldr: Week 1 — Foundations: orient to the unit, learn the call-now safety check, conduct your first psychiatric interview, structure a mental status exam, write an admission note, and ask one capacity question on rounds.
points: The skill of the week is the Mental Status Exam plus the call-now safety check — use the interactive MSE module, write your first admission note, and tell the resident or attending immediately when safety could change today.
Required Week 1 safety recognition set: suicide intent/plan/preparation/means, escalating agitation, delirium/catatonia signs, and alcohol/benzodiazepine/opioid withdrawal concern.
Suggested landmark readings: Engel 1977 (biopsychosocial), Rosenhan 1973 (labeling), and Appelbaum & Grisso 1988 (capacity) — three papers that shape how the unit thinks about diagnosis and autonomy.
On the unit this week: shadow an admission, ask one capacity question on rounds, and name one safety concern you would escalate immediately.

cta.label: Open the Interview & MSE Pocket Guide

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Open with the patient's story, then make sure suicide risk, violence risk, vulnerability, substances/withdrawal, medical contributors, and collateral needs are covered before you close.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Write one concrete example for each MSE domain instead of only using adjectives.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Escalate immediately for current suicidal intent or preparation, escalating threats/agitation, delirium/catatonia signs, withdrawal concern, or any interaction that feels unsafe.
clinicalWorkflow.say: You can choose what you answer. I do have to tell the team if there is an immediate safety concern, and my goal is to understand what would help.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask what the patient is like at baseline, what changed, when it changed, and what safety or function concerns have appeared.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Give a one-liner, the key MSE findings, the safety read, and one capacity or collateral question.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Interview/MSE questions test observation, organization, and whether you ask direct safety questions.

week2.md.tldr: Week 2 — Mood, Psychosis & Pharmacology: build a differential for depression, mania, and psychosis; learn antipsychotic-selection logic by side-effect profile; and run a Bush-Francis catatonia screen on any mute or immobile patient.
points: The skill of the week is the psychopharmacology primer — work through the top-10 inpatient classes and apply the CATIE lesson: choose antipsychotics by side-effect profile (metabolic, QTc, EPS), not by generation.
Suggested landmarks: CATIE (Lieberman 2005), STAR*D (Rush 2006), and Bush 1996 (catatonia) — Journal Clubs 1 and 5 pair with these readings.
On the unit: run a Bush-Francis catatonia screen on any mute or immobile patient — the screen is diagnostic and the lorazepam challenge can be therapeutic.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For every mood or psychosis presentation, ask about mania/hypomania, substances, sleep, medical causes, medication exposure, and catatonia signs.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Track mood/affect, thought process, delusions/hallucinations, sleep/energy, psychomotor signs, and attention.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Do not miss catatonia, delirium, withdrawal, serotonin syndrome/NMS, command hallucinations, or suicide risk.
clinicalWorkflow.say: That sounds frightening. I do not see it the same way, but I want to understand what you are experiencing and what would help you feel safer.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask family/staff about baseline, time course, sleep, substances, adherence, prior episodes, and what changed right before admission.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present syndrome, differential, safety concern, medication logic by side-effect profile, and the one mimic you still need to rule out.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Mood/psychosis questions often hinge on bipolar screening, substance/medical mimics, catatonia, and medication adverse effects.

week3.md.tldr: Week 3 — Psychotherapy, Personality & the Relationship: understand common factors, practice DBT-informed care for borderline-pattern crises, and complete a supervised collaborative safety plan using the Stanley-Brown model.
points: The skill of the week is completing a supervised safety plan with a patient using the C-SSRS — practice building it collaboratively in real time, not as a form to fill.
Suggested landmarks: Wampold 1997 (common factors) and Linehan 1991 (DBT for BPD) — Journal Club 3 (Safety Planning) ties them to the clinical week.
On the unit: draft a full biopsychosocial and relational formulation, and notice a rupture-and-repair moment in the therapeutic relationship for the Week 3 reflection.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask what crisis pattern brought the patient in, what has helped before, what invalidates or escalates, and what skill or support is missing after discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Track affective reactivity, impulse control, interpersonal stance, self-harm urges, and whether the patient can collaborate in the moment.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Collaborative safety planning is supervised clinical work; do not treat a completed form as risk resolution.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I can see why that landed as hurtful. I want to understand the impact, and then we can work together on the most accurate way to describe the crisis.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask supports about baseline risk, effective limits, outpatient continuity, crisis plans, and what tends to rupture trust.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Name the relational pattern, the current safety state, one repair move, and the discharge-continuity need.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Psychotherapy/personality questions test validation plus limits, not reassurance or jargon used at the patient.

week4.md.tldr: Week 4 — Family, Systems & Expressed Emotion: observe or co-facilitate a family meeting, spot high expressed emotion, and cite the family-intervention evidence for relapse prevention.
points: The skill of the week is the Family Meeting Playbook (90-min) — observe first, then co-facilitate with a defined role; use an expressed-emotion spotting checklist during the meeting.
Suggested landmarks: Brown 1962 (expressed emotion) and Pharoah 2010 (Cochrane family intervention) — Journal Clubs 2 and 6 pair with these.
Reflection prompt: 'What would I change about that family meeting?' — identify the phase where time was lost and debrief with your supervisor.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Before the meeting, clarify consent, purpose, family concerns, discharge tasks, and what the patient does not want discussed.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Notice patient affect, participation, shutdown, activation, and whether family criticism or over-involvement changes the room.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Do not let family anxiety or reassurance replace a concrete risk and discharge plan.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Before details, let's agree on the goal, what the patient has consented for us to discuss, and what needs to be decided before discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask for baseline, timeline, safety observations, medication/adherence barriers, and what support is realistic at home.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Report the family meeting goal, consent boundary, key collateral, discharge barrier, and next family/system task.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Family questions test confidentiality, expressed emotion, psychoeducation, and whether support actually changes risk.

week5.md.tldr: Week 5 — Acute & Emergency Psychiatry deepens the Week 1 recognition set: manage agitation safely through the verbal de-escalation ladder, distinguish delirium/catatonia/withdrawal from psychiatric symptoms, assess violence risk with structured tools, and document supervised escalation reasoning.
points: The skills of the week are the agitation ladder and Violence-Risk/Brøset tool, delirium prevention and cause search, and supervised CIWA-Ar/COWS trend interpretation — all are bedside tools available in the hub sidebar.

What is different from Week 1: Week 1 teaches spot it and call now; Week 5 asks you to explain the likely driver, try least-restrictive communication when safe, use structured tools with supervision, and document what would change the plan.
Pocket references to keep on hand: restraint checklist, benzo taper protocol, and clozapine ANC monitoring schedule.
Case of the week: substance plus psychosis plus risk composite — designed to integrate the acute safety calls covered throughout the rotation.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For acute concerns, ask what changed, what is the immediate risk, what medical/substance driver could explain it, and what has de-escalated before.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Prioritize attention, arousal, motor signs, psychosis, intoxication/withdrawal signs, and observable agitation trajectory.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Escalate early for delirium/catatonia concern, withdrawal, escalating threats, severe agitation, restraint/seclusion, or medication-toxicity signs.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I hear that this feels urgent. Tonight the safest plan is to lower stimulation, keep clear limits, and choose the next calming step together.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask nursing/family about baseline, trigger, substances, access to means, prior agitation plans, and what usually helps or worsens things.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Give the acute problem, current safety level, medical mimic, de-escalation step tried, and what would trigger senior/security/medical escalation.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Acute questions often test delirium, catatonia, withdrawal, violence risk, and least-restrictive escalation.

week6.md.tldr: Week 6 — Integration, Disposition & Exam Readiness: build a discharge/disposition plan, present a full case with formulation and risk reasoning, and complete the shelf high-yield review and OSCE station set.
points: Skills of the week: the Risk-Stratified Discharge Pathway, the shelf high-yield review with self-check, and the full OSCE station set for stations you have not yet completed.
Suggested readings: Felitti 1998 (ACE study) and Deegan 1996 (recovery) — the two papers that frame trauma and the patient's own goals in the discharge plan.
Reflection: end-of-rotation professional-identity reflection — what changed in how you think about psychiatric illness, the therapeutic relationship, and your role on the team.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For your final patients, ask what diagnosis still feels uncertain, what risk remains modifiable, and what discharge support is still unproven.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use serial MSE changes to support your formulation rather than presenting the admission snapshot as static.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Before discharge discussion, name remaining acute risk, chronic risk, means access, follow-up reliability, and what would change the plan.
clinicalWorkflow.say: We cannot promise zero risk, but we can name the specific safety steps that must be in place before discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Confirm the discharge plan with supports: medications, follow-up, means safety, supervision, transportation, warning signs, and what to do if risk escalates.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present a full case with formulation, risk reasoning, family/system plan, and the one uncertainty you would track after discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Use the patient in front of you as the shelf organizer: syndrome, mimic, treatment, safety/legal issue, and disposition.

reading_map.md.tldr: Six weeks of suggested readings paired with one clinical skill and one observable task each week — a coverage map, not a reading list; nothing here should take longer than 20 minutes.
points: Each week has a small suggested core plus optional deeper resources — the weekly skill anchor is the clinical behavior you are building toward, not the reading itself.
Week 4 is the most reading-intensive, covering the Family Meeting Playbook, family therapy modalities, and the family/discharge module — reflecting this rotation's signature focus on family work.
Week 6 reading is deliberately light because the skill of the week is a full OSCE-style case presentation integrating everything from the prior five weeks.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For the current week, identify the skill anchor, one patient-linked reading, and one observable task you can actually do on the unit.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use the weekly focus to decide what part of the MSE deserves extra attention this week.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: When a weekly task touches risk, capacity, withdrawal, delirium, catatonia, or family safety, do it with supervision rather than as a solo checklist.
clinicalWorkflow.say: This week I am practicing one clinical behavior, not trying to read everything.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use the family/systems weeks to practice permission, baseline questions, and discharge feasibility with supervision.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Bring one weekly reading into rounds as a clinical question, not a literature summary.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: The reading map is a spaced sequence; pair each week with review cards or one question-bank session.

osce.md.tldr: Six OSCE stations covering the skills most tested on rounds — suicide risk with collateral, capacity with delirium recognition, catatonia, alcohol withdrawal, family meeting agenda, and oral case presentation — with entrustment anchors 1–4.
points: Each station specifies behaviors to practice, not answers to memorize — rater focus is on clinical reasoning, communication, and appropriate escalation, not on naming the correct drug first.

Station 2 (capacity) and Station 3 (catatonia) test whether you avoid premature psychiatric labels when a medical mimic is present — both require recognizing the underlying driver before concluding behavior.
Target entrustment level 3 by end of rotation: able to perform routine parts with indirect supervision and escalate appropriately — safe and organized, not yet independent.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For each OSCE station, first identify the task: risk, capacity, catatonia, withdrawal, family meeting, or oral presentation.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use observable MSE findings to justify your next step; stations reward saying what you saw, not only naming a diagnosis.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: State when you would stop the station and get supervision, medical evaluation, or emergency support.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I want to ask this directly because safety matters: have you had thoughts of killing yourself?
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use collateral to test baseline, time course, risk, and discharge feasibility rather than asking for global impressions.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Give a concise assessment, your immediate safety action, and the data that would change your plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Practice stations aloud: opening line, core questions, safety escalation, and summary.

cases.md.tldr: Eight synthetic composite cases spanning first-episode mania, suicide risk, withdrawal, delirium, catatonia, family dynamics, and discharge planning — each includes student tasks, hidden clinical detail that rewards direct questioning, and a case discussion template.
points: Each case contains hidden clinical detail that is only revealed when the student asks directly — the reward for thorough, non-assumption-based history-taking.
Student tasks mirror the OSCE: build the differential, name the safety questions, draft an MSE, prepare a family meeting agenda, and identify the discharge barrier.
The case discussion template asks: what would change the differential? what collateral is missing? what is the discharge barrier? what must be done before tomorrow? — use it after every case.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For each case, ask what hidden detail would change diagnosis, risk, disposition, or family/system plan.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Document the MSE finding that most changes the differential and the one finding that could be misleading.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Name the safety question before the diagnosis question when the case includes suicide, violence, withdrawal, delirium, catatonia, or discharge risk.
clinicalWorkflow.say: What is he like at baseline, what changed, when did it change, and what specific safety concerns have you noticed?
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use collateral to define baseline, timeline, safety, adherence, supports, and discharge barriers.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: After the case, present problem representation, differential, risk formulation, collateral gap, and next action.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Synthetic cases are practice for illness scripts: syndrome, mimic, first-line treatment, safety/legal issue, and disposition.

shelf.md.tldr: Use patients to organize exam review — for each patient, name the syndrome, write the differential, name one medical mimic, name first-line treatment, and name one safety or legal issue; the exam is patient-anchored, not topic-anchored.
points: Six COMAT/shelf exam traps to internalize: 'denies SI — low risk' (ask about means and preparatory behavior), 'psychosis means schizophrenia' (check substances, mood, and delirium first), and 'family support means discharge is safe' (family support is data, not a risk decision).

The final week 9-item checklist covers mania vs. stimulant intoxication, delirium vs. psychosis, capacity in 4 abilities, chronic vs. acute risk formulation, catatonia red flags, antipsychotic adverse effects, lithium monitoring, alcohol withdrawal risk, and case presentation under 6 minutes.

Legal and ethical questions anchor on decision-specific capacity, duty-to-protect jurisdictional variation, and voluntary vs. involuntary hospitalization — treat these as clinical reasoning problems, not rule memorization.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Turn each patient into an exam stem: age, time course, syndrome, key risk, mimic, and next best step.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Translate MSE into exam language: attention for delirium, psychomotor change for catatonia/mania, thought process/content for psychosis.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Shelf traps often hide safety in plain sight: means access, preparatory behavior, delirium, withdrawal, capacity, and adverse medication effects.
clinicalWorkflow.say: My answer is..., because the discriminating feature is..., and the tempting wrong answer misses...
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use collateral facts as exam discriminators: baseline, timeline, adherence, substance exposure, family safety, and follow-up feasibility.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Rehearse one 20-second answer before rounds, then test the same concept in the question bank.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Study by patient problem, not topic list: syndrome, mimic, treatment, safety/legal, and disposition.

book_library.md.tldr: Curated from 345 titles for the inpatient rotation — use the library to go deeper on a patient's diagnosis or recommend a book to a family; domains span borderline, addiction, trauma, mood, psychosis, ADHD, and child development.
points: Books in the library double as bibliotherapy recommendations — pick by the patient and family in front of you, not by diagnostic category alone.

Highest-yield family resources: CRAFT approach (Beyond Addiction) for substance use, LEAP method (I Am Not Sick I Don't Need Help!) for psychosis anosognosia, and Stop Walking on Eggshells for borderline-pattern family dynamics.
For trauma: The Body Keeps the Score is the standard patient/family resource; for mood narratives: An Unquiet Mind (bipolar) and Reasons to Stay Alive (depression) are widely received and readable.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Pick one patient or family question first; then choose a book that fits their stage, literacy, culture, and immediate clinical need.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use narratives to understand meaning, shame, identity, ambivalence, and family burden rather than only diagnostic facts.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Do not present a book as treatment, crisis care, or a substitute for the team; avoid recommendations that could increase shame or conflict.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Offer resources with permission: 'Some families find this useful; would it be okay if I shared it as one optional support?'
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask whether the family prefers practical guides, lived-experience narratives, or brief handouts before recommending anything.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Mention a book recommendation only when it supports psychoeducation, engagement, or discharge planning.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Link books to clinical themes: LEAP and anosognosia, CRAFT and substance use, family burden, trauma narratives, and stigma.

podcast_library.md.tldr: Dr. David Puder's Psychiatry & Psychotherapy Podcast — 250+ episodes in 10 categories with YouTube links; start with the therapeutic alliance series (Ep. 28/32/36/62/69) and use the library as a point-of-care reference matched to your patient panel.
points: The Foundations section (38 episodes) covers psychiatric interview, therapeutic alliance, suicide, capacity, and Big Five personality — the highest-yield cluster for the clinical rotation.
Full episode pages and CME credit are available at psychiatrypodcast.com; YouTube links are provided for direct access without subscription or download.
Start with a patient in front of you and find the category that matches today's clinical question — use it as a point-of-care resource rather than listening linearly.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Start from a live clinical question, then choose one short episode or clip that helps you ask a better question today.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use interview and alliance episodes to improve observation of affect, stance, defenses, rupture, and the patient's experience of the interview.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Do not listen during patient care or use podcast content as a protocol; confirm safety and medication decisions with faculty and local standards.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Convert what you learn into one patient-centered phrase or one question you will try on the unit.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use collateral-focused episodes to sharpen what you ask and what you avoid disclosing without consent.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Bring one concise learning point when it improves the assessment, formulation, or medication conversation.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Use podcast notes as an entry point, then test yourself with active recall or the question bank.

landmark_trials.md.tldr: Fifty landmark papers as 90–120 second audio overviews with board-style self-test in Shelf Mode and Daily Review — listen to the four Foundations papers first (Engel, Rosenhan, Robins-Guze, Insel), then follow your patients to the theme that fits.
points: Each audio is 90–120 seconds — short enough for the walk between the unit and the staff room, not a dedicated study block.

The Acute & Safety cluster (6 papers) covers Appelbaum capacity, Bush-Francis catatonia, lithium-suicide (Cipriani 2013), safety planning (Stanley 2012), and the limits of risk-factor prediction (Franklin 2017) — the most rotation-relevant papers.

The same trials feed the board-style questions in Shelf Mode and Daily Review, which extend beyond the individual trial into the broader clinical question — pair the audio with those for shelf preparation.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Choose the paper that answers the clinical problem in front of you: capacity, catatonia, lithium-suicide, safety planning, or diagnostic validity.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Separate what the study measured from what you observed at bedside; do not let a trial result replace the individual assessment.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Use safety papers to support supervision and documentation, not to independently clear or detain a patient.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Translate one landmark finding into a plain-language explanation only when it helps shared decision-making.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use paper themes to guide collateral questions about timeline, prior response, safety environment, and treatment adherence.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Offer a 20-second evidence pearl when it changes the differential, risk formulation, or next step.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Pair each audio with board-style self-test in Shelf Mode or Daily Review, then answer one question bank item on the same concept.

rounds_questions.md.tldr: Nearly 100 Q&A pairs formatted for oral rehearsal before rounds — each with a model answer, supporting evidence, key paper, and clinical pearl; rehearse out loud, not by reading silently.
points: The format mirrors what attendings actually ask: a direct clinical question, a concise evidence-based answer, the key paper, and one pearl that adds depth or names a trap.
Covers all shelf/COMAT domains: psychotic disorders (Q1–15), mood, substance use, acute safety, personality, neurocognitive, and psychopharmacology.
Rehearse out loud before rounds — saying the answer in 20–30 seconds approximates the actual clinical demand and reveals gaps that silent reading conceals.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Before rounds, pick one likely attending question from the patient in front of you: diagnosis, risk, medication, family, disposition, or evidence.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Tie your answer to today's observed MSE change, not just to a memorized fact.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: When a question touches suicide, violence, delirium, catatonia, withdrawal, capacity, or medication toxicity, include what would trigger escalation.
clinicalWorkflow.say: My current answer is..., and the piece of data that would change my mind is...
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use collateral to support or challenge the answer: baseline, time course, adherence, side effects, family safety, and outpatient course.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Answer in one sentence, then add evidence or a clinical pearl only if it changes the plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Oral rehearsal improves retrieval: say the answer out loud, then test the same concept in the question bank.

omm_resources.md.tldr: OMM/OPP competencies in psychiatry are taught and checked by your osteopathic faculty — this page points to AACOM and AOA resources; the evidence base is emerging and limited, and OMM should be framed as adjunctive, not established first-line.
points: OMM objectives for the psychiatry rotation focus on structural exam for somatic dysfunction tied to anxiety, insomnia, and autonomic dysregulation — gentle techniques (suboccipital release, rib raising, diaphragmatic release) are the target skills.
The mechanistic rationale is autonomic balance shift toward parasympathetic tone; the evidence is emerging — mostly small pilot studies — so present it as adjunctive rather than established.
Document your osteopathic reasoning in the assessment when anxiety, insomnia, or chronic pain are present — that is what the OPP competency is looking for in the note.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Ask whether anxiety, insomnia, pain, autonomic arousal, or somatic distress are clinically relevant before considering an OPP frame.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Observe posture, tension, breathing, psychomotor activation, and distress while keeping the psychiatric assessment primary.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: OMM is adjunctive here; it does not replace evidence-based psychiatry, medical workup, emergency care, or attending supervision.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Ask permission before any body-based discussion or intervention and describe it as optional supportive care.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Clarify prior osteopathic care, trauma history, touch preferences, pain history, and what has helped regulate distress.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Document osteopathic reasoning briefly when it changes the assessment or plan, and defer technique details to trained faculty.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Know the competency frame: structural exam, autonomic rationale, adjunctive role, and limits of the evidence base.

rotation.md.tldr: A week-by-week map of the four-week inpatient block: safety and the acute workup first, then diagnosis and psychopharmacology, then systems and med-legal, then integration, supervision, and scholarship.
points: Week 1 builds the acute-safety base (suicide, violence, agitation, capacity, withdrawal, delirium, catatonia) while you start carrying patients.
Weeks 2–3 deepen diagnosis and prescribing, then move from the patient to the system (commitment, capacity, documentation, disposition).
Week 4 is leading rounds, supervising the student, and consolidating — pick a case or topic to present.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Anchor each week to one resident-level job: stabilize acute safety, sharpen diagnosis, manage systems/legal work, then lead and teach.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Track how MSE findings evolve across the admission and how they change level of care, medications, privileges, and discharge readiness.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Escalate early for suicide, violence, withdrawal, delirium, catatonia, capacity, seclusion/restraint, and involuntary-treatment questions.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Practice giving patients and families a resident-level explanation of the plan that is clear, bounded, and aligned with attending supervision.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Make collateral a daily workflow: baseline, risk, medication history, prior admissions, family capacity, and discharge barriers.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Lead with an assessment that names uncertainty, risk, and the next decision the team must make.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Use the four-week map to link ward cases to board-style concepts without letting exam prep crowd out clinical ownership.

adv_psychopharm.md.tldr: Sequence therapy rationally, recognize genuine first-line failure, escalate to definitive treatment (clozapine, ECT) without delay, and own the safety monitoring that keeps patients alive between doses.
points: "Treatment-resistant" is a measurement claim: confirm adequate dose and duration, verify adherence, and track with a repeated scale before escalating.
Two failed adequate antipsychotic trials defines treatment-resistant schizophrenia — clozapine is the only superior agent and is started too late; do not keep cycling.
Build monitoring at order entry: lithium renal/thyroid/PTH, clozapine ANC + bowel regimen, antipsychotic metabolic panel, QTc when stacking.
adv_psychopharm.md.cant: Clozapine-associated constipation can progress to a fatal ileus — a bowel regimen is part of the prescription; and smoking cessation induces CYP1A2, so a patient who quits at admission may need a dose decrease, not an increase.

quiz.q: A patient with schizophrenia has failed two adequate antipsychotic trials with documented adherence. Best next step?

o.t: Try a third first-line second-generation antipsychotic
Start clozapine with ANC and metabolic monitoring
Add a benzodiazepine and reassess in a month
Combine two antipsychotics at high dose

quiz.why: Two failed adequate trials defines treatment-resistant schizophrenia, where clozapine is the only agent with demonstrated superiority; cycling further agents or high-dose combinations just delays the effective treatment.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Before escalating, verify the measurement claim: adequate dose, adequate duration, adherence, diagnosis, comorbidity, and a repeated symptom scale.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Tie medication changes to target symptoms and observed function, not only the diagnosis name.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Own monitoring at order entry: ANC, bowel regimen, metabolic labs, QTc, lithium renal/thyroid/PTH, pregnancy considerations, withdrawal risks, and local protocols.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Explain escalation plainly: what failed, why this next step is different, what monitoring protects against, and what the patient can refuse or ask.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask about prior trials, side effects, adherence barriers, smoking changes, constipation, access, family concerns, and outpatient monitoring feasibility.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present the medication plan as target symptom, evidence rationale, safety monitoring, and contingency.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Know high-yield thresholds and first-line failures: clozapine after two adequate antipsychotic trials, ECT indications, lithium monitoring, serotonin syndrome vs NMS.

cl_reference.md.tldr: The numbers residents carry on the consult service: serotonin syndrome vs NMS, the catatonia lorazepam challenge, lithium-toxicity thresholds, and QTc action points — recognition and escalation, confirmed against institutional protocol.
points: Serotonin syndrome is fast with clonus and hyperreflexia; NMS is slow with lead-pipe rigidity and CK often >1,000 — tempo and the neuromuscular exam separate them.
Catatonia: a ≥50% BFCRS drop after a 2 mg IV lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic; avoid antipsychotics; ECT is definitive.
Lithium: toxicity generally ≥1.5 mEq/L, dialysis if >4.0 (or >2.5 with severe signs) — treat the patient, not the number, in chronic toxicity.
cl_reference.md.cant: In serotonin syndrome, physical restraints are contraindicated — isometric contraction worsens hyperthermia and lactic acidosis; sedate instead.
ruleOut: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (lead-pipe rigidity, high CK, slow onset)
cl_reference.md.firstMove: Stop the offending agent, cool and support, give a benzodiazepine, and match the antidote to the syndrome — cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, dantrolene/bromocriptine for severe NMS.

quiz.q: A patient on a serotonergic agent develops rapid-onset hyperthermia with lower-extremity clonus and hyperreflexia. Best next step?

o.t: Apply physical restraints for safety
Start an antipsychotic to control agitation
Stop the agent, sedate with a benzodiazepine, and give cyproheptadine
Give dantrolene for presumed NMS

quiz.why: Clonus and hyperreflexia with fast onset are serotonin syndrome: stop the agent, cool/support, benzodiazepine, cyproheptadine. Restraints worsen hyperthermia, antipsychotics can worsen it, and dantrolene targets NMS (slow onset, rigidity, high CK).

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Use consult references to recognize the syndrome, stop the offending exposure, stabilize first, and call the right help early.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Prioritize tempo, attention, arousal, neuromuscular findings, autonomic instability, rigidity, clonus, tremor, and fluctuating consciousness.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: These are escalation syndromes; confirm medication, restraint, transfer, antidote, and dialysis decisions with supervising physicians and institutional protocols.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Keep patient explanations brief and concrete during emergencies: what is happening, what the team is doing now, and who is being called.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Clarify medication timing, dose changes, substances, infection/medical triggers, baseline cognition, and prior reactions.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present consult problems as syndrome, evidence, immediate risk, next test or treatment, and escalation plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Differentiate serotonin syndrome, NMS, malignant catatonia, lithium toxicity, delirium, and withdrawal by tempo and exam findings.

systems_medlegal.md.tldr: Your documentation, your handling of voluntary/involuntary status, and your disposition planning are clinical acts with legal weight — do them deliberately and verify every statute-specific detail against current Maine law (Title 34-B) and hospital policy.
points: Document the reasoning behind risk and observation level, not just a score — most patients who die by suicide screen low-risk at last contact.
An involuntary hold is not authorization to medicate over objection; non-emergency forced medication needs its own legal/administrative process.
Disposition starts at admission: least-restrictive level of care, a dated follow-up ≤7 days, a warm handoff, and problem-solving boarding/housing/guardianship.
systems_medlegal.md.cant: "Hold" is not "treat": verify the Maine/hospital pathway for medication over objection before treating a refusing patient, and document the emergency rationale when you medicate to prevent imminent harm.

quiz.q: A patient on an emergency involuntary hold refuses their scheduled antipsychotic (no emergency). What is correct?

o.t: The hold authorizes you to medicate over objection
Discharge the patient for non-cooperation
Sedate them involuntarily to enforce the order
Respect the refusal and pursue the separate legal process for medication over objection

quiz.why: Commitment and involuntary medication are distinct: a hold does not authorize non-emergency medication over objection, which requires its own legal/administrative pathway. Emergency medication is only for imminent harm.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: For every med-legal question, ask what authority is being used, what risk it addresses, what less-restrictive option was considered, and what local policy requires.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Document the mental-status facts that support capacity, risk, voluntariness, insight, judgment, and ability to participate in discharge planning.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Never treat a hold as permission for non-emergency medication over objection; confirm statutes, hospital policy, and attending direction.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Explain limits plainly: what is voluntary, what is required for safety, what information can be shared, and what choices remain available.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Use minimum-necessary disclosure, clarify consent when possible, and gather only information that changes diagnosis, risk, treatment, or discharge.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Present the legal status, decision-making capacity, safety rationale, family contact plan, and disposition barrier as separate items.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Know the distinction between capacity and competence, commitment and medication over objection, confidentiality and duty to protect, and risk factors versus formulation.

supervision_teaching.md.tldr: You sit in the middle of the supervision chain — earning graduated autonomy from your attending while becoming the first-line supervisor for the MS3 — on the shared skills of explicit expectations, active feedback, and knowing when to ask for help.
points: Entrustment is graded (observe → direct → indirect → oversee); over four weeks, earn indirect supervision on specific activities, not vaguely "get better."
Teach with the One-Minute Preceptor (get a commitment, probe reasoning, teach one principle, reinforce, correct) and give feedback via Ask–Tell–Ask.
Keep formative feedback distinct from summative evaluation, and treat asking for help as a professionalism competency, not a weakness.
supervision_teaching.md.cant: "Agree with above" over an exam you did not perform is both a quality and a liability problem — document your own independent assessment; the attending remains the physician of record.

quiz.q: A student presents a case and you want to teach effectively in one minute. What comes first?

o.t: Get a commitment — ask what they think is going on
Deliver the correct answer so they learn it
Point out every error in the presentation
Give general praise to build confidence

quiz.why: The One-Minute Preceptor starts by getting a commitment so the learner reasons first; you then probe the reasoning and teach to the gap. Leading with the answer, error-listing, or vague praise skips the diagnostic step and teaches less.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: At the start of a task, name the expected level of supervision, what you will do independently, and when you will call for help.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Teach students to support MSE claims with observed behavior, direct quotes, and what changed from yesterday.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Supervision boundaries are patient-safety boundaries; uncertainty, high-risk communication, restraint, legal status, and medication refusal need escalation.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Use Ask-Tell-Ask for feedback and the One-Minute Preceptor to make the learner reason before you teach.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Coach students to get permission, ask a focused question set, avoid over-disclosure, and return with a 30-second update.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Model a concise assessment, then give one reinforcing point and one correction after the student presents.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Use teaching moments to connect bedside reasoning with board-style distinctions without turning rounds into a lecture.

canon_200.md.tldr: A residency-level reading canon — a Top 25 essential set plus subdomain lists across psychopharmacology, psychotherapy, anxiety/OCD, PTSD, suicide, neuroscience, neuromodulation, addiction, eating disorders, and nosology — used across training, not in four weeks.
points: The Top 25 (STAR*D, CATIE, Cipriani 2018, the ACE study, NCS-R, and more) are the conceptual scaffolding of modern psychiatry.
The MS3 site's 50-paper landmark set is the starting subset; this canon extends it to residency-level depth.
Use it longitudinally across training — pick a subdomain that matches your current rotation or scholarly interest.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Choose one paper by the patient, rotation, or scholarly question in front of you; do not try to consume the canon linearly.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use landmark papers to sharpen concepts, then return to the specific patient's observed symptoms, function, and context.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Do not use historical or trial summaries as local protocol; verify high-risk clinical decisions with current guidelines and supervision.
clinicalWorkflow.say: Practice explaining a complex evidence idea in one clear sentence before using it with patients, families, or students.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Let the reading generate better questions about longitudinal course, prior treatment response, family history, trauma, and systems barriers.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Bring a canon paper only when it helps the team make a sharper diagnostic, risk, or treatment decision.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Use the Top 25 as a longitudinal board-study spine, then reinforce with active recall and question-bank practice.

collateral_workflow.md.tldr: Collateral is clinical data, not gossip: get permission when possible, ask only what changes diagnosis/risk/treatment/discharge, share the minimum necessary, and bring one clear update back to the team.
points: Start with a one-sentence purpose: baseline/timeline, safety, treatment history, or discharge reality.
Use consent and minimum-necessary disclosure; when uncertain, disclose less and ask the supervising team.
Return with a 30-second team update: source, baseline, timeline, risk data, discharge barrier/support, and what changes in the plan.
collateral_workflow.md.cant: Do not promise discharge, share more than consent/local policy permits, or document family opinions as facts without attribution.

quiz.q: A student calls a parent for collateral and opens by summarizing the full diagnosis and medication plan before asking any questions. What should the student have done first?

o.t: Share the diagnosis first so the parent understands the clinical frame
Ask whether the parent agrees with the patient being hospitalized
State role and purpose, clarify disclosure boundaries, then ask targeted baseline/timeline/risk/discharge questions
Avoid collateral because family reports are often biased

quiz.why: Collateral calls should start with role, purpose, and confidentiality boundaries. The student can gather clinically useful data without over-disclosing protected information.

clinicalWorkflow.ask: Name the purpose before calling: baseline/timeline, risk, treatment history, or discharge reality.
clinicalWorkflow.mse: Use collateral to clarify baseline cognition, behavior, affect regulation, psychosis, sleep, substances, and function.
clinicalWorkflow.safety: Ask about suicide, violence, means access, vulnerability, supervision limits, and what would make discharge unsafe.
clinicalWorkflow.say: I may not be able to share details without permission, but I can listen and bring relevant information back to the team.
clinicalWorkflow.collateral: Ask targeted buckets: baseline/timeline, risk/safety, treatment/function, and discharge reality.
clinicalWorkflow.rounds: Report source, baseline, timeline, risk-relevant data, discharge barrier/support, and what changes in the plan.
clinicalWorkflow.exam: Collateral is used to test timeline, risk, capacity, delirium/dementia, mania/psychosis, substance use, and discharge realism.

toxidromes.md.tldr: Four hyperthermic emergencies share fever + altered mental status + autonomic instability; the neuromuscular exam, the skin, and the last 72 h of medication changes separate them and dictate sharply different treatment.
points: Lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia after a dopamine blocker → NMS; clonus + hyperreflexia, legs>arms, after a serotonergic agent → serotonin syndrome.
Dry, flushed skin + mydriasis + urinary retention → anticholinergic toxicity; waxy flexibility/posturing without a clear drug trigger → malignant catatonia (ECT is definitive).
Reconstruct every medication change in the last 72 hours — that history usually names the syndrome.
toxidromes.md.cant: Never give an antipsychotic to a rigid, febrile patient in NMS or malignant catatonia — antipsychotics are the cause, not the treatment; stop the offending agent, cool and support, and escalate.
toxidromes.md.firstMove: Stop the likely offending agent, support and cool aggressively, send a CK, and rule out infection/heat stroke — then discriminate by reflexes and skin.

med_monitoring.md.tldr: Every psychotropic with a monitoring requirement has a baseline and an ongoing schedule; ordering the labs, β-hCG, and EKG before the first dose and tracking the next level is concrete bedside safety work.
points: Lithium: 12-h trough drawn ~5 days after any dose change; target ≈ 0.6–1.0 (up to ~1.2 in acute mania); NSAIDs/thiazides/ACE-inhibitors raise levels.
Clozapine ANC weekly ×6 mo → every 2 wk ×6 mo → monthly (per prescribing information; FDA eliminated the REMS in 2025); myocarditis is the early killer.
Valproate and lithium are teratogens — β-hCG before starting; carbamazepine needs CBC/LFTs/sodium, HLA-B*1502 in at-risk ancestry, and watch for SIADH.
med_monitoring.md.cant: Do not treat monitoring as optional or after-the-fact — baseline and ongoing metabolic labs, β-hCG, and a QTc before QT-prolonging agents are part of the prescription.

psychotherapy.md.tldr: You won't run a course of therapy on a 5-day admission, but you're expected to match the modality to the problem, recognize the patient it fits, and use the supportive stance in every encounter.
points: BPD/recurrent self-harm → DBT; OCD/phobia → CBT with exposure and response prevention; grief- or transition-linked depression → IPT.
Supportive psychotherapy is the default inpatient stance; psychodynamic/insight work is the wrong tool for an acutely psychotic, manic, or cognitively impaired patient.
Psychotherapy and medication are usually additive, not either/or.
psychotherapy.md.cant: Don't attempt uncovering/insight work with an acutely ill patient — it can destabilize; validate and support instead.

case_formulation.md.tldr: A formulation answers why this patient, why now — built on the biopsychosocial axis and sharpened by the four P's (predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective) — and turns a diagnosis into a plan.
points: The differential gives the diagnosis; the formulation gives the 'why now' and the plan.
Always name a precipitant ('why now?') and at least one protective factor — the two cells students most often skip.
Every perpetuating factor is a treatment target; every protective factor is a lever.
case_formulation.md.cant: Don't stop at a diagnosis or write an all-biology story — force a psychological and a social contributor into the formulation.

medical_workup.md.tldr: A new psychiatric presentation is a medical workup until proven otherwise — rule out the medical and substance mimics before committing to a psychiatric diagnosis.
points: Red flags: first episode at an atypical age, no prior psychiatric history, abnormal vitals or a focal neuro exam, visual hallucinations, and fluctuating attention (delirium until proven otherwise).
Core new-admission screen: vitals, CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, UA, urine tox + alcohol, β-hCG before medications, and a baseline QTc before QT-prolonging agents.
Psychosis + movement disorder + seizures/autonomic instability → think anti-NMDA-receptor (autoimmune) encephalitis.
medical_workup.md.cant: Don't inherit 'psych' as the label on an older or medically ill patient with an acute change — take the vitals and test attention yourself first.
medical_workup.md.firstMove: Take the vitals and test attention yourself, order the core labs + β-hCG + QTc, and present the medical differential first when the story is 'new, old, and abnormal-vitals.'

anki.md.tldr: Download the clerkship's attested question bank and high-yield concepts as Anki spaced-repetition decks; suspend all cards, then unsuspend by topic as the rotation covers each block.
points: Two decks, both built only from attested content: the Question Bank (vignette cards) and Concepts (topic one-liners + high-yield pearls, with author-bolded facts as cloze deletions).
Import the combined .apkg for one file with both subdecks; every card is tagged by topic, source page, high-yield, and attestation status for the suspend/unsuspend workflow.
Decks regenerate automatically on each site rebuild, so they stay in sync with the library.
